scenes.title: Torque to motion
scenes.brief: A chapter map as a machine: on the left an orange torque dial per joint, in the middle a blue two-link arm (live twoLink dynamics), on the right a pink hand chasing a gold dot. Clicking a station lights the path torque → dynamics → motion → feedback, and a split toggle shows the same task planned in joint space (orange) or hand space (pink). A final slate wall station shows the hand pressing it with a purple contact arrow. A family-tree strip at the bottom links each station to the scene that goes deeper.

scenes.title: Energy to motion
scenes.brief: Teal beads constrained to slate wires: purple constraint arrows appear perpendicular to each wire and only tangential motion survives. A knob panel collapses 3n bead coordinates into m orange generalized-coordinate dials. Two bars show T (blue) and V (slate) with L = T − V; Lagrange's rule is animated as momentum bar slope versus force bar. Finale: a 3D spherical pendulum whose θ, φ dials drive the bob, with the energy bar flat and a trail on the sphere.

scenes.title: Spin laziness
scenes.brief: A blue blob of teal mass particles with a gold balance-point dot that slides as you paint mass. Spin it with an orange ω arrow: each particle shows a speed bar and a kinetic-energy meter sums ½ρ|ω×r|². The inertia tensor appears as an ellipsoid whose axes are principal axes; a resizable bar (drag l, w, h) shows the three diagonal numbers m(w²+h²)/12 etc. updating. Last, a 6×6 grid lights mI and I blocks, and moving the frame off the center of mass makes coral off-diagonal blocks appear.

scenes.title: Two-link swing
scenes.brief: A planar blue two-link arm with orange joints and teal center-of-mass dots. Drag joint speeds: teal velocity arrows on each center of mass update, and a 2×2 heat grid shows M(θ) with α, β, δ entries (β·cos θ2 pulsing as the elbow bends). Spin joint 1 alone and watch a coral Coriolis/centrifugal torque appear at joint 2. Final mode: orange torque sliders drive dynamics.twoLinkAccel live, with the energy readout matching work done.

scenes.title: Push and spin
scenes.brief: A blue brick floating in slate space. Push its gold center of mass with a teal force arrow: it accelerates without turning. Spin it about each principal axis: stable about the long and short axes, tumbling about the middle one, with a ω×Iω coral arrow shown. Toggle the camera between the world frame (I′ = RIRᵀ changes) and riding on the brick (I fixed, but ω×mv appears). Final panel stacks force and torque into one 6-vector wrench and shows the 6×6 block equation driving the brick.

scenes.title: Arm mass matrix
scenes.brief: An n-link blue arm whose links each carry a teal 6×6 inertia block; their Jacobian-weighted sum JᵢᵀMᵢJᵢ stacks into the orange n×n M(θ) heat grid that reshapes as you drag joints. Gold center-of-mass heights fill a slate potential bar. A Christoffel cube Γᵢⱼₖ lights the cells contributing to each Coriolis term. The full equation is shown as four colored torque bars (inertial, Coriolis, gravity, applied) that always sum to zero. Last beat: a power meter shows θ̇ᵀ(Ṁ−2C)θ̇ pinned at zero while the arm swings freely.

scenes.title: Twists to dynamics
scenes.brief: A 3D three-link elbow arm with orange joint twist axes. Each link's teal body Jacobian columns are drawn as twist arrows transported by the adjoint (Ad) from the joint to that link's center of mass. A matrix panel builds M(θ) as Σ AᵢₗᵀMₗAₗ products and C from Lie-bracket terms. Swapping to an idealized SCARA arm shows M with a constant diagonal-like block as the arm moves, with only the in-plane coupling term changing.

scenes.title: Ball in bowl
scenes.brief: A phase plane with a gold equilibrium dot. Drag a teal start point; its trajectory streams out. Two lime circles ε and δ let you play the stability game: pick ε, find δ so the trajectory never leaves ε. A bowl-shaped blue surface V sits over the plane; a ball rolls with an energy bar that only goes down (V̇ ≤ 0) or strictly down (V̇ < 0). An exponential envelope e^(−αt) curve overlays the distance plot to show the rate.

scenes.title: Zoom and look
scenes.brief: A nonlinear vector field with a magnifier: zooming into the gold equilibrium straightens the arrows into the linear field Ax. Eigenvalues of A appear as dots in the complex plane: all left (lime) → stable, any right (coral) → unstable, on the axis (purple) → can't tell. Example tabs: an undamped spring-mass whose phase orbits are ellipses with a flat energy bar; a damped one spiraling in; and a cubic spring where V = ½ẋ² + spring energy still bowls.

scenes.title: Where it settles
scenes.brief: A phase plane where trajectories leave fading trails; their tails accumulate into a gold ω-limit set (a point or a loop). Invariant sets glow as lime regions trajectories never leave. A teal stripe marks where V̇ = 0; the animation shows trajectories sliding along it but only being able to stay at the gold equilibrium. Applied to a damped nonlinear spring: V̇ = −bẋ² vanishes on the whole ẋ = 0 axis, but only the origin is invariant.

scenes.title: Cancel and steer
scenes.brief: A blue two-link arm with a gold ghost arm following θd(t) along a gold path. The control torque is split into a blue model bar (M θ̈d + Cθ̇ + N) and an orange feedback bar (M(−Kv ė − Kp e)). With the model exact, the coral error plot is a clean decaying second-order response matching poles you place on a slider. A mismatch slider scales the model's mass and the error stops being linear, leaving a coral residual.

scenes.title: PD plus gravity
scenes.brief: The arm joints are drawn with orange coil springs to gold setpoints and teal dashpots. An energy bar shows ½θ̇ᵀMθ̇ + ½eᵀKpe falling monotonically while the arm settles; the drop rate equals the damper's θ̇ᵀKvθ̇. A LaSalle overlay marks the θ̇ = 0 set and shows only the target is invariant. Last beat: a moving gold trajectory with feedforward, an augmented energy-plus-cross-term bar proving tracking.

scenes.title: Steer the hand
scenes.brief: The same arm, but the knob is the pink hand: drag a gold target and the controller pulls the hand along a straight line. A side panel shows the hand-space inertia ellipse M̃ = J⁻ᵀMJ⁻¹ that flattens near a singularity (🚫 flash). Step-response race: a joint-space computed-torque hand (orange trail, curved) versus a workspace computed-torque hand (pink trail, straight) to the same gold goal.

scenes.title: Arm in a slot
scenes.brief: A two-link arm whose pink hand rides in a slate slot. Allowed directions glow lime along the slot, forbidden ones coral across it; a purple λ arrow shows the slot pushing back. A splitter shows the joint torque decomposed into a motion part (moves along the slot) and a force part (presses into the wall). Gold targets: a position along the slot and a desired push force; two meters (position error, force error) both drop to zero.

scenes.title: Dynamics challenges
scenes.brief: A challenge board of locked tiles, one per exercise, each opening a challenge mode inside the chapter's scenes: make an inertia ellipsoid match a target, derive a toy system's torque bars until the simulation matches, find a V whose bar never rises, or tune gains so the arm hits a gold target. Lime check when the live readout meets the gold condition.

pages.summary: Chapter opener: derive open-chain equations of motion with twists, then use their structure to build tracking controllers; actuators are idealized as pure torque sources.

atoms.idea: Chapter 4 title: Robot Dynamics and Control.

The chapter derives the equations of motion of a general open-chain arm, writing the kinematics with twists, and then exploits the structure of those equations to design controllers that drive the arm onto a desired trajectory.
atoms.feynman: Knowing how a swing responds to pushes (dynamics) lets you time your pushes so it goes exactly as high as you want (control).
atoms.visual: Opening station of the roadmap: an orange torque dial feeds a blue arm, the arm's motion feeds a gold trajectory checker, and a loop arrow closes back to the dial. Each block lights in turn.

atoms.idea: Section 4.1 Introduction.
Kinematics alone assumed any joint trajectory could be commanded and would be obeyed exactly; this chapter asks how to actually make a real arm execute a given joint path.
atoms.feynman: A drawing of a dance is not the dance: someone still has to push the legs at the right moments with the right strength.
atoms.visual: A gold ghost arm sweeps a planned path; a blue real arm released with zero torque just sags under gravity, revealing the gap that dynamics and control must close.

atoms.idea: Actuators (electric, hydraulic, pneumatic) apply torques or forces at the joints. Dynamics maps those torques to motion. Actuator dynamics are ignored, so any joint torque can be commanded instantly.
atoms.feynman: Pretend every joint has a perfect hand-crank: whatever twist you ask for, you get immediately, with no motor lag.
atoms.visual: Each orange joint has a torque slider that acts instantly (no ramp); the arm's angular acceleration arrow responds in the same frame the slider moves.

atoms.idea: Page 155.

pages.summary: Why use a Lagrangian derivation, why feedback is needed, joint-space versus workspace control, contact deferred; Section 2 begins.

atoms.idea: The arm's motion obeys nonlinear second-order ODEs fixed by its kinematics and mass properties. Rather than summing every force on every link, the chapter uses Lagrange's method, which needs only kinetic and potential energy and exposes useful structure.
atoms.feynman: To predict a roller coaster you can track every push on every bolt, or just track height and speed (energy); the energy bookkeeping is far harder to get wrong.
atoms.visual: Two columns race to the same answer: on the left a tangle of coral force arrows on each link, on the right just a blue T bar and a slate V bar. Both produce the same blue arm motion; the right side finishes first.

atoms.idea: Control is the inverse problem: choose torques so the arm follows a trajectory. A perfect model would give torques directly, but real systems need feedback that corrects for initial errors, sensor noise and model error.
atoms.feynman: Walking with eyes closed works only if your map of the room is perfect; opening your eyes (feedback) lets you fix every small drift.
atoms.visual: Toggle eyes-closed vs eyes-open: in open-loop the blue arm, given a slightly wrong mass, drifts off the gold path (coral gap grows); with feedback the coral gap shrinks back to zero.

atoms.idea: The main problem treated is position regulation and tracking. Joint-space control turns the task into joint paths and tracks them; workspace control writes the controller directly in end-effector position and orientation.
atoms.feynman: To draw a line you can either plan each finger joint's motion, or just watch your pen tip and steer it.
atoms.visual: Split screen: left, orange joint-angle plots driving the arm (joint space); right, the pink hand dragged toward a gold dot with its own error arrow (workspace). The hand paths differ in shape.

atoms.idea: Harder still is contact with the environment, where both position and applied force must be regulated; treated briefly at chapter end and fully in Chapter 6.
atoms.feynman: Wiping a table: you must move the cloth along the surface and press down just hard enough at the same time.
atoms.visual: A slate wall appears; the pink hand slides along it while a purple push arrow into the wall is held at a gold target length.

atoms.idea: Section 4.2 Lagrange's Equations.
Many derivation methods give equivalent equations in different forms; the Lagrangian route, built on energy, is chosen because it gives closed-form equations suited for analysis.
atoms.feynman: Many roads lead to the same city; pick the road with the clearest signposts.
atoms.visual: Three path icons (forces, virtual work, energy) all end at the same gold equation box; the energy path is highlighted.

atoms.idea: Page 156.

pages.summary: Particles obeying Newton's law, holonomic constraints g(r)=0, and constraint forces along the constraint gradients scaled by Lagrange multipliers.

atoms.idea: Continuation: the energy-based method yields closed-form equations that permit detailed analysis.
atoms.feynman: A recipe written down once can be studied, scaled and tweaked, unlike cooking by feel.
atoms.visual: The gold equation box from the previous page opens to reveal colored terms that can be inspected one by one.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.2.1 Basic formulation.

atoms.label: Eq (4.1)
atoms.idea: Start from n point masses each obeying Newton: force equals mass times acceleration, F_i = m_i r̈_i with r_i in R³.
atoms.feynman: Push a shopping cart harder and it speeds up faster; push a heavier one and it speeds up slower.
atoms.visual: Free teal beads on a slate table; drag a force arrow onto one and its acceleration arrow is the force scaled by 1/m (bead size).

atoms.label: Eq (4.2)
atoms.idea: Linked particles are restricted by constraints g_j(r_1..r_n) = 0. Constraints that are algebraic in positions only are holonomic; velocity-dependent ones appear later with fingers.
atoms.feynman: Beads threaded on a wire can only be where the wire is: the wire is a rule about position.
atoms.visual: Teal beads snap onto slate wires; dragging a bead off the wire is impossible (coral flash), along it is free (lime). A second mode adds a rolling-disk constraint shown greyed as 'later'.

atoms.label: Eq (4.3)
atoms.idea: Constraint forces keep g = 0 satisfied. They are normal to the constraint surface, so the system equation becomes F = (block-diagonal mass) r̈ + Σ Γ_j λ_j, with Γ_j a basis of constraint-force directions, e.g. the gradients of g_j.
atoms.feynman: A bead on a curved wire: the wire pushes sideways on the bead just enough to keep it on, never along the wire.
atoms.visual: A bead slides on a curved slate wire under gravity; a purple arrow along the wire's normal (gradient of g) changes length every frame to keep the bead on the wire, while the lime tangent shows the allowed motion.

atoms.idea: The λ_j are Lagrange multipliers. Solving 3n+k equations in r and λ determines them; λ gives only relative magnitudes since the Γ_j need not be unit length.
atoms.feynman: How hard the wire pushes is a number you only learn by solving, and it depends on how long you drew the normal arrow.
atoms.visual: A λ meter beside the purple arrow; rescaling the drawn normal Γ doubles its length and halves λ, with the actual force unchanged.

atoms.idea: Page 157.

pages.summary: Generalized coordinates parametrize the constrained configuration; generalized forces are joint torques; the Lagrangian L = T − V; Theorem 4.1 Lagrange's equations.

atoms.label: Eq (4.4)
atoms.idea: Tracking all particles plus constraints is wasteful. Instead pick m = 3n − k generalized coordinates q with smooth maps r_i = f_i(q) that automatically satisfy every constraint.
atoms.feynman: A puppet with a hundred beads on strings is controlled by just a few sticks: move the sticks and every bead follows.
atoms.visual: A panel of 3n grey bead sliders collapses into m orange knobs; turning a knob moves all teal beads together along their wires, and a counter shows 3n − k.

atoms.idea: For a rigid-link robot the generalized coordinates are almost always the joint angles, which uniquely fix every particle's position.
atoms.feynman: Tell someone your shoulder and elbow angles and they know exactly where every bit of your arm is.
atoms.visual: A blue two-link arm with two orange knobs; the arm's every point moves as only the knobs turn.

atoms.idea: External forces are projected onto the generalized coordinates as generalized forces; for joint-angle coordinates these are the joint torques.
atoms.feynman: Pushing on a door anywhere only matters through how much it twists the hinge.
atoms.visual: Drag a teal push arrow anywhere on the arm; each orange joint shows the torque it causes (the push projected through Jᵀ).

atoms.idea: The Lagrangian is kinetic minus potential energy, L(q, q̇) = T(q, q̇) − V(q), both expressed in generalized coordinates.
atoms.feynman: A skateboarder in a half-pipe trades height for speed; the Lagrangian is the speed-energy minus the height-energy.
atoms.visual: A skateboarder in a slate half-pipe with a blue T bar and slate V bar; a gold L bar shows their difference swinging positive and negative as it rolls.

atoms.label: Thm 4.1
atoms.idea: Lagrange's equations: for each coordinate, the time rate of change of ∂L/∂q̇_i minus ∂L/∂q_i equals the external generalized force Υ_i.
atoms.feynman: How fast your momentum changes equals the push you get from the hill plus any push from outside.
atoms.visual: For a pendulum: a teal momentum bar ∂L/∂q̇ with its slope drawn live, a slate bar ∂L/∂q, and an orange Υ bar; the slope always equals the slate bar plus orange bar.

atoms.label: Eq (4.5)
atoms.idea: Vector form: d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q = Υ.
atoms.feynman: The same rule for every knob at once, stacked in a column.
atoms.visual: The single-coordinate bar triple from above is copied once per orange knob and stacked into a column.

atoms.idea: Page 158.

pages.summary: Spherical pendulum figure; Lagrange's equations reduce the equation count and restate Newton's law (rate of momentum = force); Example 4.1 set up.

atoms.label: Fig 4.1
atoms.idea: A point mass on a massless rod of length l from a ball joint, configured by polar angle θ from the vertical and azimuth φ about it, under gravity mg.
atoms.feynman: A tetherball on its rope: one angle says how far out it swings, the other says which way around the pole.
atoms.visual: 3D: a slate pivot, a blue rod, a teal bob; orange arcs for θ (from vertical) and φ (around), and a gold mg arrow down.

atoms.idea: The partial-derivative terms and Υ are formally row vectors (covectors) though written as columns; a proof of Thm 4.1 is in standard mechanics texts.
atoms.feynman: A force reading and a velocity look alike on paper but are different kinds of things, like a price tag and a shopping list.
atoms.visual: Velocity arrows drawn teal as columns, force-like ∂L/∂q drawn as orange rows; their dot product gives a power number.

atoms.idea: Lagrange reduces the equations from one per particle to one per generalized coordinate. With no constraints and q = r it gives back F = m r̈. Rearranged, it reads: rate of change of generalized momentum equals generalized force.
atoms.feynman: Whether you count every grain of sand in a bucket or just the bucket, swinging it obeys the same push-equals-momentum-change rule.
atoms.visual: A cloud of free teal beads: toggle 'no constraints' and the Lagrange bars become plain F = m a bars per bead; toggle constraints back and the bars merge into fewer knob bars.

atoms.label: Ex 4.1
atoms.idea: Example setup: spherical pendulum of mass m and length l, angles θ and φ; find its motion under gravity.
atoms.feynman: A tetherball given a sideways shove: predict its looping path.
atoms.visual: Spherical pendulum loaded with drag handles for initial θ, φ and their speeds; play button runs it.

atoms.idea: Page 159.

pages.summary: Spherical pendulum: position, kinetic and potential energy, Lagrangian, partial derivatives and the resulting coupled equations (4.7); start of rigid-body inertial properties.

atoms.label: Eq (4.6)
atoms.idea: Bob position: r = l(sin θ cos φ, sin θ sin φ, −cos θ).
atoms.feynman: Latitude and longitude on a globe hung upside-down tell where the bob is.
atoms.visual: The bob rides on a translucent blue sphere of radius l; θ and φ dials move it, with xyz numbers in red/green/blue.

atoms.idea: Energies: T = ½ml²(θ̇² + sin²θ φ̇²), V = −mgl cos θ, so L = T − V.
atoms.feynman: Swinging around the pole fast is easy when the ball is far out and pointless when it hangs straight down: the sin²θ factor.
atoms.visual: Blue T and slate V bars; hold θ near 0 and spin φ̇: the T bar barely grows. Tilt to θ = 90° and the same φ̇ fills it.

atoms.idea: Partials: d/dt ∂L/∂θ̇ = ml²θ̈; ∂L/∂θ = ml² sinθ cosθ φ̇² − mgl sinθ; d/dt ∂L/∂φ̇ = ml² sin²θ φ̈ + 2ml² sinθ cosθ θ̇φ̇; ∂L/∂φ = 0.
atoms.feynman: Spinning a ball on a string flings it outward (centrifugal) while gravity pulls it back down.
atoms.visual: Each partial appears as a colored bar on the pendulum: orange centrifugal outward arrow from φ̇², slate gravity arrow, coral coupling term. A note: φ never appears in L, so its momentum bar stays constant.

atoms.label: Eq (4.7)
atoms.idea: Equations of motion: diag(ml², ml² sin²θ)(θ̈, φ̈) plus velocity-product terms plus (mgl sin θ, 0) equals zero; with initial conditions they fix the motion uniquely.
atoms.feynman: Give the tetherball one shove and its whole dance is decided.
atoms.visual: Run: the bob traces a rosette on the sphere; a flat blue+slate energy bar and a constant teal azimuthal-momentum bar confirm conservation.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.2.2 Inertial properties of rigid bodies.
To apply Lagrange to a robot we need each link's kinetic and potential energy as functions of joint angles and speeds.
atoms.feynman: To know how hard an arm is to swing, you need to know how its weight is spread out.
atoms.visual: Each blue link glows with a teal mass-density shading, hinting that its energy will be computed from that spread.

atoms.idea: Page 160.

pages.summary: Mass distribution, total mass and center of mass; the kinetic energy of a moving body as a volume integral of ½ρ|ṗ + Ṙr|².

atoms.label: Fig 4.2
atoms.idea: Frames for kinetic energy: inertial frame A and a body frame B at the center of mass, with g the body's pose and r a body point.
atoms.feynman: A sticker on a spinning frisbee: we describe it from the ground and from the frisbee.
atoms.visual: A slate world frame and a blue body with its own red/green/blue axes at a gold center-of-mass dot; a teal point r on the body.

atoms.idea: Each link is a rigid body, so its energies are determined by total mass and moments of inertia about its center of mass.
atoms.feynman: A hammer's swing feel is set by its weight and where that weight sits.
atoms.visual: Two blue sticks of equal mass, one with weight at the tip; spin both with the same ω and compare their energy bars.

atoms.idea: Mass is the volume integral of density: m = ∫ ρ(r) dV (constant ρ for homogeneous bodies).
atoms.feynman: Weigh a cake by adding up every crumb.
atoms.visual: Paint teal density on a blue blob with a brush; a mass counter adds up the painted cells.

atoms.idea: Center of mass: r̄ = (1/m) ∫ ρ(r) r dV, the density-weighted average position.
atoms.feynman: The spot where you can balance a plate on one finger.
atoms.visual: As you paint density, a gold balance dot slides to the weighted mean; a finger-tip icon under it balances the blob level.

atoms.label: Eq (4.8)
atoms.idea: With the body frame at the center of mass and pose (p, R), a body point moves with velocity ṗ + Ṙr, so T = ½ ∫ ρ |ṗ + Ṙr|² dV.
atoms.feynman: Kinetic energy of a moving body is the sum of the zoom-energy of each of its crumbs.
atoms.visual: The blob slides and spins; every teal particle shows its own velocity arrow ṗ + Ṙr; a blue T meter sums ½ρ|v|².

atoms.idea: Expand the square: |ṗ|² + 2ṗᵀṘr + |Ṙr|² inside the integral.
atoms.feynman: Total jiggle = slide part + mixed part + spin part.
atoms.visual: The T meter splits into three stacked colored segments: slide (blue), cross (coral), spin (orange).

atoms.idea: Page 161.

pages.summary: Cross term vanishes at the center of mass; rotational energy ½ωᵀIω defines the inertia tensor; total energy ½VᵀMV with the 6×6 generalized inertia matrix.

atoms.idea: The cross term disappears because ∫ ρ r dV = 0 when the body frame sits at the center of mass.
atoms.feynman: Spin a plate about its balance point and the parts going one way exactly cancel those going the other.
atoms.visual: Move the body frame: the coral cross-term segment of the T meter is zero only when the frame origin sits on the gold center-of-mass dot; slide it away and it grows.

atoms.idea: Spin term: Ṙr = R ω̂ r = −R r̂ ω, so ½∫ρ|Ṙr|² = ½ ωᵀ(−∫ρ r̂² dV) ω = ½ ωᵀ I ω with body angular velocity ω.
atoms.feynman: How hard it is to spin something depends on how far each crumb is from the spin axis, squared.
atoms.visual: Orange ω arrow through the blob; each teal particle's speed bar is |ω × r|; the summed spin energy equals ½ωᵀIω shown by a blue ellipsoid whose radius in ω's direction sets the number.

atoms.idea: The inertia tensor I = −∫ρ r̂² dV is symmetric, with diagonals like Ixx = ∫ρ(y²+z²) and off-diagonals like Ixy = −∫ρ xy.
atoms.feynman: Each diagonal number says how lazy the body is to spin around one axis; off-diagonals say spinning around one axis makes it want to tip around another.
atoms.visual: A 3×3 heat grid beside the blob; painting mass far from the x axis brightens Ixx; painting an off-axis diagonal smear lights the coral Ixy cells and tilts the ellipsoid.

atoms.label: Eq (4.9)
atoms.idea: Total kinetic energy = ½m|ṗ|² + ½ωᵀIω = ½(Vᵇ)ᵀ M Vᵇ with body twist Vᵇ and the 6×6 block-diagonal generalized inertia M = diag(mI, I), symmetric positive definite.
atoms.feynman: The energy of a thrown frisbee is its flying-energy plus its spinning-energy, added in one 6-number ledger.
atoms.visual: A 6-vector twist (teal v, orange ω) multiplies a 6×6 grid lit as two diagonal blocks; the result fills the blue T meter. Any twist gives a positive bar.

atoms.label: Ex 4.2
atoms.idea: Example setup: a homogeneous rectangular bar of mass m and sides l, w, h; density m/(lwh).
atoms.feynman: A chocolate bar: same stuff everywhere, so its density is just weight divided by size.
atoms.visual: A blue box with orange drag handles on l, w, h; a density readout updates.

atoms.idea: Page 162.

pages.summary: Bar inertia tensor computed by integration: diagonal entries m(w²+h²)/12 etc., zero products of inertia, and the block-diagonal 6×6 matrix (depends on CoM frame).

atoms.label: Fig 4.3
atoms.idea: A homogeneous rectangular bar with a center-of-mass frame aligned to its edges (lengths l along x, w, h).
atoms.feynman: A brick with a skewer through its middle along each edge.
atoms.visual: Blue box with red/green/blue axes through its gold center; dimension labels as single symbols l, w, h.

atoms.idea: Density is m/(lwh), and the frame is placed at the center of mass aligned with the bar's principal axes.
atoms.feynman: Put the skewer exactly in the middle and along the brick's edges, so nothing wobbles.
atoms.visual: Snap the axes to the box center: a lime check appears when origin = center and axes = edges.

atoms.idea: Integrating gives Ixx = m(w² + h²)/12, while Ixy = −(m/lwh)∫xy dV = 0 by symmetry.
atoms.feynman: Spinning a brick around its long axis only fights the short sides; mirror-image crumbs cancel in the mixed terms.
atoms.visual: Slice the box into thin teal slabs; each slab's (y²+z²) contribution stacks into the Ixx bar; for Ixy, paired mirror crumbs flash + and − and cancel to 0.

atoms.idea: Full tensor: I = (m/12) diag(w²+h², l²+h², l²+w²), diagonal because the axes are principal.
atoms.feynman: A long thin pencil is easy to twirl along its length, hard end-over-end.
atoms.visual: Drag l longer: the green and blue diagonal cells grow, red stays put; the ellipsoid stretches accordingly. A twirl test spins the bar with the same torque about each axis to show who spins fastest.

atoms.idea: Generalized inertia: M = diag(m, m, m, Ixx, Iyy, Izz); the block-diagonal form depends on putting the frame at the center of mass (Exercise 3).
atoms.feynman: Pushing and twirling the brick are separate jobs only if you hold it at its balance point.
atoms.visual: The 6×6 grid is diagonal; drag the frame origin off the gold center and coral off-diagonal blocks m·p̂ light up, coupling push and spin.

atoms.idea: Page 163.

pages.summary: Two-link planar arm: links as bars with diagonal inertias; kinetic energy as a sum of link terms; center-of-mass positions and velocities from the kinematics.

atoms.label: Fig 4.4
atoms.idea: Two-link planar arm with link lengths l1, l2, joint angles θ1, θ2 and center-of-mass distances r1, r2 from each joint.
atoms.feynman: Your upper arm and forearm swinging on a tabletop.
atoms.visual: Blue links, orange joints with θ arcs, teal center-of-mass dots at r1 and r2 along each link.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.2.3 Example: dynamics of a two-link planar robot.
Model each link as a homogeneous bar with mass m_i and diagonal inertia at its center of mass; total T is the sum over links of ½m_i|v_i|² + ½ω_iᵀI_iω_i.
atoms.feynman: The arm's motion energy is the forearm's plus the upper arm's, each with a slide part and a spin part.
atoms.visual: Each link shows its own two-segment energy bar (blue slide, orange spin); a total bar stacks all four.

atoms.idea: Motion is planar, so v_i is in the xy plane and ω_i is along z with magnitudes θ̇1 and θ̇1 + θ̇2.
atoms.feynman: The forearm spins as fast as the shoulder plus the elbow.
atoms.visual: Spin indicators: link 1 rotates at θ̇1, link 2 at θ̇1+θ̇2 (two orange dials adding into one).

atoms.idea: Center-of-mass positions and velocities: p1 = r1(c1, s1), p2 = l1(c1, s1) + r2(c12, s12), with velocities by differentiation.
atoms.feynman: Where your elbow points and how fast it moves depends on the shoulder; the forearm's middle depends on both joints.
atoms.visual: Drag joint speeds; teal velocity arrows on each center-of-mass dot update live and decompose into shoulder (orange 1) and elbow (orange 2) contributions.

atoms.idea: Page 164.

pages.summary: Two-link kinetic energy as ½θ̇ᵀM(θ)θ̇ with constants α, β, δ, the resulting equations (4.11); Newton–Euler section motivated by the lack of a global parametrization of SE(3).

atoms.label: Eq (4.10)
atoms.idea: Summing link energies gives T = ½θ̇ᵀM(θ)θ̇ with M = [[α + 2β c2, δ + β c2], [δ + β c2, δ]], where α, β, δ are combinations of masses, lengths and inertias.
atoms.feynman: A folded arm is easier to spin at the shoulder than a straight one: the inertia depends on the elbow angle through cos θ2.
atoms.visual: A 2×2 heat grid shows M(θ); bend the elbow and the top-left cell (α + 2β c2) dims as the arm folds. Hovering α, β or δ highlights which links' masses feed it.

atoms.label: Eq (4.11)
atoms.idea: Substituting L = T into Lagrange's equations gives M(θ)θ̈ + C(θ, θ̇)θ̇ = τ, where C is built from β sin θ2 times joint speeds.
atoms.feynman: Push on the shoulder and elbow and the arm answers with accelerations set by how heavy it currently feels.
atoms.visual: Orange torque sliders at both joints drive dynamics.twoLinkAccel live; the blue arm swings and the bars for inertial, coral velocity and orange applied torque always balance; the energy readout tracks the work done by the sliders.

atoms.idea: Reading the terms: the first is inertial (joint accelerations), the second Coriolis and centrifugal, the right side the applied torques.
atoms.feynman: Swing your upper arm fast and your forearm gets flung outward, even if your elbow muscles do nothing.
atoms.visual: Spin joint 1 at constant speed with joint 2 limp: a coral Coriolis/centrifugal torque bar at joint 2 grows as β s2 θ̇1², flinging the forearm outward.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.2.4 Newton-Euler equations for a rigid body.

Lagrange assumes the configuration space can be parametrized by an open subset of Rⁿ. SE(3) needs local coordinates such as Euler angles, and every such chart is singular somewhere, so the result is only local.
atoms.feynman: Any flat map of the Earth tears or stretches somewhere; a globe has no such seam.
atoms.visual: Spin the blue brick with Euler-angle dials: at gimbal lock a 🚫 flash shows two dials doing the same thing, so the Lagrange equations in those coordinates blow up there.

atoms.idea: The goal instead: a global description of rigid-body dynamics under external force and torque, first classically and then with twists and wrenches.
atoms.feynman: Use the globe, not the map.
atoms.visual: The Euler dials fade out and a coordinate-free 6-vector (twist) panel fades in beside the brick.

atoms.idea: Setup: g = (p, R) is the pose of a frame at the center of mass; a force f acts at the center of mass, expressed in the inertial frame.
atoms.feynman: Push a floating box exactly at its balance point.
atoms.visual: Gold center-of-mass dot on the blue brick, slate world axes, and a teal f arrow attached at the dot.

atoms.idea: Page 165.

pages.summary: Translational motion f = m p̈ independent of rotation; angular momentum about the center of mass with I′ = RIRᵀ leads to Euler's equation I′ω̇ + ω × I′ω = τ.

atoms.label: Eq (4.12)
atoms.idea: Newton for the center of mass: f = d/dt(m ṗ) = m p̈, unaffected by rotation because the center of mass is used as the reference point.
atoms.feynman: Throw a spinning wrench: its balance point flies in a clean parabola no matter how it tumbles.
atoms.visual: Toss the blue brick with random spin under gravity: it tumbles wildly but its gold center-of-mass dot traces a perfect slate parabola.

atoms.idea: For rotation, torque equals the rate of change of angular momentum I′ωˢ, with I′ = R I Rᵀ the inertia tensor seen from the world frame and ωˢ the spatial angular velocity.
atoms.feynman: A figure skater's spin-momentum depends on how her arms are oriented right now, seen from the audience.
atoms.visual: The brick's inertia ellipsoid rotates with the brick; from the world view its matrix numbers keep changing even though the body is unchanged.

atoms.label: Eq (4.13)
atoms.idea: Differentiate R I Rᵀ ωˢ, use ṘRᵀ = ω̂ˢ, and cancel the I′ωˢ × ωˢ-type term to get Euler's equation: I′ω̇ˢ + ωˢ × I′ωˢ = τ.
atoms.feynman: A spinning object whose spin axis is not a balance axis has to keep being pushed to stay on track; the extra push is the ω × Iω term.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) momentum arrow I′ω; (2) it changes because ω changes and because the ellipsoid rotates; (3) the rotation part appears as a coral ω × I′ω arrow. Demo: spin the brick about its middle axis with τ = 0 and watch it flip (tennis-racket effect).

atoms.idea: Note: (f, τ) here is in inertial coordinates about the moving center of mass, so it is not a wrench in the earlier sense, and (ṗ, ωˢ) is neither the spatial nor body twist.
atoms.feynman: Measuring a moving car's speed with a ruler nailed to the road gives numbers that are about the car but not in the car's own language.
atoms.visual: The world-frame (f, τ) pair is drawn dashed-coral beside a true spatial wrench in solid colors; they disagree unless the brick sits at the world origin.

atoms.idea: Page 166.

pages.summary: Newton and Euler rewritten in body coordinates and stacked into the 6-D Newton–Euler equation (4.16) driven by a body wrench.

atoms.idea: Continuation: likewise (ṗ, ωˢ) does not match the spatial or body velocity.
atoms.feynman: Same object, mixed languages.
atoms.visual: Teal ṗ and orange ωˢ arrows shown next to a proper body twist; a mismatch coral flash marks the difference.

atoms.label: Eq (4.14)
atoms.idea: With body velocity vᵇ = Rᵀṗ and body force fᵇ = Rᵀf, Newton becomes m v̇ᵇ + ωᵇ × m vᵇ = fᵇ.
atoms.feynman: Riding on a merry-go-round, a ball rolling straight looks like it curves: that apparent curving is the ω × v term.
atoms.visual: Ride-along camera on the spinning brick: the gold center moves straight in the world, but in the body view its velocity arrow turns, explained by a coral ωᵇ × m vᵇ arrow.

atoms.label: Eq (4.15)
atoms.idea: Euler in body coordinates: I ω̇ᵇ + ωᵇ × Iωᵇ = τᵇ, where the inertia I is now constant.
atoms.feynman: On the skater's own body, her shape doesn't change when she turns; only the world sees it rotating.
atoms.visual: Body-view toggle: the inertia ellipsoid freezes (constant numbers) while the world view shows it rotating.

atoms.label: Eq (4.16)
atoms.idea: Stacked: diag(mI, I)(v̇ᵇ, ω̇ᵇ) + (ωᵇ × mvᵇ, ωᵇ × Iωᵇ) = Fᵇ, the body Newton–Euler equation; global, and linear and angular motion couple.
atoms.feynman: A thrown spinning football's flight and spin are tied together when seen from the ball's own seat.
atoms.visual: A 6-vector wrench (teal force, orange torque) feeds the 6×6 block grid; the brick integrates the equation; coupling terms flash coral whenever both v and ω are nonzero.

atoms.idea: A spatial-frame version also exists (Exercises 4 and 5) with similar coupling; the book uses the body form throughout.
atoms.feynman: You can narrate a dance from the stage or from the audience; pick one and stick to it.
atoms.visual: A toggle body/spatial: both give the same brick motion; the body version is highlighted as the default.

atoms.idea: Page 167.

pages.summary: Open-chain Lagrangian: link frames at centers of mass, link body Jacobians, link kinetic energies and the manipulator inertia matrix M(θ) = ΣJᵢᵀMᵢJᵢ.

atoms.idea: Section 4.3 Dynamics of Open-Chain Manipulators.
Use the product-of-exponentials kinematics to write the Lagrangian in joint variables and extract properties needed for control stability proofs.
atoms.feynman: Once you know how each joint moves each piece of the arm, you can add up the arm's energy.
atoms.visual: The arm from the kinematics chapter reappears with orange twist axes; energy bars start appearing on each link.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.3.1 The Lagrangian for an open-chain robot.

Attach frame Lᵢ at link i's center of mass; its pose is g_sli(θ) = e^{ξ̂1θ1}…e^{ξ̂iθi} g_sli(0). Its body velocity is Jᵢ(θ)θ̇, where the body Jacobian's columns are the joint twists (up to i) expressed in the link frame, and later columns are zero.
atoms.feynman: The forearm moves when the shoulder or elbow turns, but not when the wrist does if the forearm sits before the wrist.
atoms.visual: Select link i: its Jacobian columns appear as teal twist arrows for joints 1..i, the rest greyed zero; dragging a joint speed shows how each column contributes to that link's velocity.

atoms.label: Eq (4.17)-(4.18)
atoms.idea: Link energy Tᵢ = ½θ̇ᵀJᵢᵀMᵢJᵢθ̇; total T = Σ Tᵢ = ½θ̇ᵀM(θ)θ̇.
atoms.feynman: The whole arm's swing energy is the sum of each piece's.
atoms.visual: Per-link energy bars stack into one total bar; a lime check confirms total equals ½θ̇ᵀMθ̇ computed from the grid.

atoms.label: Eq (4.19)
atoms.idea: The manipulator inertia matrix: M(θ) = Σᵢ Jᵢᵀ(θ) Mᵢ Jᵢ(θ).
atoms.feynman: Each link's heaviness, seen through how the joints move it, piles into one table of how hard the arm is to accelerate.
atoms.visual: Animated sum: each link's 6×6 teal block is sandwiched by its Jacobian and lands as a colored layer in the orange n×n M grid; drag joints and the layers reshape.

atoms.idea: Page 168.

pages.summary: Gravity potential from link center-of-mass heights completes L = ½θ̇ᵀMθ̇ − V; Lagrange's equations applied term by term.

atoms.idea: Potential energy: Vᵢ = mᵢ g hᵢ(θ), heights of centers of mass; V = Σ mᵢ g hᵢ(θ).
atoms.feynman: Lifting your arm costs energy proportional to how high each heavy part goes.
atoms.visual: Gold dots at each link's center of mass with vertical slate height rulers; a slate potential bar sums mᵢghᵢ as you raise the arm.

atoms.idea: Lagrangian of the arm: L = ½θ̇ᵀM(θ)θ̇ − V(θ).
atoms.feynman: Swing-energy minus lift-energy.
atoms.visual: Blue T bar and slate V bar side by side with a gold L bar showing the difference.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.3.2 Equations of motion for an open-chain manipulator.

atoms.label: Eq (4.20)
atoms.idea: Write kinetic energy as a double sum ½ΣMᵢⱼθ̇ᵢθ̇ⱼ so that derivatives can be taken entrywise.
atoms.feynman: Unpack the energy table into individual cells so you can poke each one.
atoms.visual: The M grid explodes into cells, each multiplied by its pair of orange speed dials.

atoms.idea: Apply Lagrange: d/dt ∂L/∂θ̇ᵢ = Σⱼ(Mᵢⱼθ̈ⱼ + Ṁᵢⱼθ̇ⱼ), ∂L/∂θᵢ = ½Σ ∂Mₖⱼ/∂θᵢ θ̇ₖθ̇ⱼ − ∂V/∂θᵢ; Υᵢ collects actuator and other nonconservative torques.
atoms.feynman: The arm's momentum changes because it speeds up and because its heaviness itself shifts as it bends.
atoms.visual: Two colored bars per joint: blue Mθ̈ and coral Ṁθ̇ (from the grid changing while the arm bends); slate gravity bar beside.

atoms.idea: Page 169.

pages.summary: Equations of motion with Christoffel symbols Γᵢⱼₖ; inertial, Coriolis/centrifugal, potential and external pieces; external forces split into torques and −N (gravity, friction).

atoms.idea: Expanding Ṁᵢⱼ via the chain rule gives Σ Mᵢⱼθ̈ⱼ + Σ (∂Mᵢⱼ/∂θₖ − ½∂Mₖⱼ/∂θᵢ)θ̇ⱼθ̇ₖ + ∂V/∂θᵢ = Υᵢ.
atoms.feynman: How the heaviness changes in time is how it changes per joint angle times how fast the joints move.
atoms.visual: Each Ṁᵢⱼ cell decomposes into a sum of ∂Mᵢⱼ/∂θₖ cells times orange θ̇ₖ dials.

atoms.label: Eq (4.21)-(4.22)
atoms.idea: Symmetrize: Σ Mᵢⱼθ̈ⱼ + Σ Γᵢⱼₖθ̇ⱼθ̇ₖ + ∂V/∂θᵢ = Υᵢ with Christoffel symbols Γᵢⱼₖ = ½(∂Mᵢⱼ/∂θₖ + ∂Mᵢₖ/∂θⱼ − ∂Mₖⱼ/∂θᵢ).
atoms.feynman: A recipe card for every pair of joint speeds: how much does spinning these two together push on this joint.
atoms.visual: A 3D cube of cells Γᵢⱼₖ; picking joint i lights a slab; each cell's glow shows how strongly speeds j and k together shove joint i.

atoms.idea: Four pieces: inertial (acceleration), Coriolis and centrifugal (quadratic in speeds), potential (∂V/∂θ), and external Υ.
atoms.feynman: Moving an arm you feel its heaviness, its fling, its weight, and your muscles.
atoms.visual: Four stacked colored torque bars per joint: blue inertia, coral velocity, slate gravity, orange applied; they always sum to zero.

atoms.idea: These velocity terms come from using non-inertial generalized coordinates: θ̇ᵢθ̇ⱼ (i ≠ j) terms are Coriolis, θ̇ᵢ² terms are centrifugal; Γ are the Christoffel symbols of M.
atoms.feynman: On a spinning merry-go-round, walking outward pushes you sideways (Coriolis); just riding pushes you out (centrifugal).
atoms.visual: In the cube, diagonal cells (j = k) are tagged with a spinning-out icon (centrifugal) and off-diagonal ones with a sideways-swerve icon (Coriolis).

atoms.idea: Split external forces into actuator torque τᵢ and −Nᵢ(θ, θ̇), covering gravity and friction (e.g. −∂V/∂θᵢ − βθ̇ᵢ for viscous friction); end-effector forces enter through the Jacobian transpose.
atoms.feynman: Your muscles push, gravity and the joint's stickiness push back, and anything you touch pushes through your arm.
atoms.visual: Add a friction slider β: a teal damping bar −βθ̇ joins the slate gravity bar inside N; drag a teal force onto the hand and its Jᵀ-reflected torques appear at the joints.

atoms.idea: Page 170.

pages.summary: Coriolis matrix C, the vector equation M θ̈ + Cθ̇ + N = τ, and Lemma 4.2: M symmetric positive definite and Ṁ − 2C skew-symmetric, with proof.

atoms.label: Eq (4.23)
atoms.idea: Coriolis matrix: Cᵢⱼ = Σₖ Γᵢⱼₖθ̇ₖ, so C(θ, θ̇)θ̇ gives the velocity forces. Other choices of C give the same product, but this one has special structure.
atoms.feynman: Many ways to split a restaurant bill give the same total; one split has a neat symmetry we will use later.
atoms.visual: C grid shown filled from the Γ cube contracted with θ̇; a 'reshuffle' button changes C to another valid choice (same Cθ̇ bar) but breaks the skew test shown later (coral).

atoms.label: Eq (4.24)
atoms.idea: The arm equation: M(θ)θ̈ + C(θ, θ̇)θ̇ + N(θ, θ̇) = τ, a second-order vector ODE from torques to motion.
atoms.feynman: Push = heaviness × acceleration + fling + weight & stickiness.
atoms.visual: Final full-arm mode: orange torque sliders in, blue arm motion out, with the four torque bars balancing every frame.

atoms.label: Lemma 4.2
atoms.idea: Structural properties: (1) M(θ) is symmetric positive definite; (2) Ṁ − 2C is skew-symmetric.
atoms.feynman: An arm is always some amount heavy in every direction, and the fling forces never create or destroy energy on their own.
atoms.visual: Two indicators: M's inertia ellipse is always a fat lime ellipse (never flat); a power meter for θ̇ᵀ(Ṁ − 2C)θ̇ stays pinned at zero while the arm swings.

atoms.idea: Positive definiteness: kinetic energy ½θ̇ᵀMθ̇ is zero only when the arm is at rest.
atoms.feynman: Anything moving has motion energy.
atoms.visual: Drag any θ̇ direction: the T bar is always positive unless all speed dials are zero.

atoms.idea: Skew symmetry: expanding (Ṁ − 2C)ᵢⱼ leaves Σₖ(∂Mₖⱼ/∂θᵢ − ∂Mᵢₖ/∂θⱼ)θ̇ₖ, which flips sign when i and j swap. It depends on the specific choice of C.
atoms.feynman: A trade where whatever I gain you lose leaves the total unchanged.
atoms.visual: Staircase: show Ṁ grid, subtract 2C grid, the result's cells light in mirrored pairs coral/lime with opposite values and a zero diagonal.

atoms.idea: Page 171.

pages.summary: Passivity interpretation of Ṁ − 2C skew; Example 4.3 three-link manipulator: twists, link frames and link inertia matrices.

atoms.label: Fig 4.5
atoms.idea: Three-link open-chain elbow arm with link lengths l0, l1, l2, center-of-mass offsets r0, r1, r2, and frames S, L1, L2, L3.
atoms.feynman: A desk lamp: a turning base, a shoulder and an elbow.
atoms.visual: 3D blue arm on a slate base; orange joint axes (one vertical, two horizontal), teal center-of-mass dots, frame triads at each.

atoms.idea: Skew-symmetry is called passivity: without friction, total energy is conserved (Exercise 8), and many control proofs depend on it.
atoms.feynman: A swing without friction keeps the same total energy forever; nothing inside it secretly pumps energy in.
atoms.visual: Free swing with τ = 0: the blue + slate total-energy bar stays perfectly flat while T and V trade back and forth.

atoms.label: Ex 4.3
atoms.idea: Example: dynamics of the three-link elbow arm; joint twists are the elbow-manipulator twists from Chapter 3.
atoms.feynman: Write down which way each joint of the desk lamp turns, and where its axis sits.
atoms.visual: Orange twist axes appear one by one on the 3D arm, each with its 6 numbers shown in a column.

atoms.idea: Link frames at centers of mass, aligned with principal axes, at reference positions (0, r0), (0, r1, l0), (0, l1 + r2, l0).
atoms.feynman: Place a tiny compass at the balance point of each lamp piece.
atoms.visual: Frame triads snap to the teal center-of-mass dots in the home pose.

atoms.idea: Each link inertia matrix is diagonal: Mᵢ = diag(mᵢ, mᵢ, mᵢ, Ixᵢ, Iyᵢ, Izᵢ).
atoms.feynman: Each piece needs just its weight and three spin-laziness numbers.
atoms.visual: Each link carries a small 6-cell diagonal strip (three teal mass cells, three orange inertia cells).

atoms.idea: Page 172.

pages.summary: Three-link example: link body Jacobians, inertia matrix entries (block structure, missing inertias), and the Christoffel formula for C.

atoms.idea: Body Jacobians J1, J2, J3 for the three links, each with nonzero columns only up to that link, entries in sines and cosines of θ2, θ3.
atoms.feynman: The base link only feels the base turning; the last link feels all three joints.
atoms.visual: Three 6×3 grids light progressively: J1 has one live column, J2 two, J3 three; drag θ2, θ3 and the cells' values breathe.

atoms.idea: M(θ) = J1ᵀM1J1 + J2ᵀM2J2 + J3ᵀM3J3.
atoms.feynman: Add up each piece's heaviness as felt at the joints.
atoms.visual: Three translucent layers stack into the 3×3 orange M grid.

atoms.idea: Entries: M11 depends on θ2, θ3 through squared sines and cosines; M12 = M13 = 0 (base decouples); M22, M23, M33 depend only on θ3 through cos θ3.
atoms.feynman: Turning the lamp's base is harder when the arm is stretched out; base turning and arm lifting don't push on each other.
atoms.visual: M grid with M12, M13 cells permanently dark; stretch the arm out and M11 brightens; bend the elbow and M22, M23 pulse with cos θ3.

atoms.idea: Some link inertias never appear because the arm's limited freedom never spins a link about certain axes.
atoms.feynman: If a door only swings on its hinge, how hard it is to twirl end-over-end never matters.
atoms.visual: Unused inertia cells on each link's strip grey out with a 'never used' slate tint.

atoms.idea: The Coriolis matrix follows from M by the Christoffel formula Cᵢⱼ = Σ Γᵢⱼₖθ̇ₖ; the computation is lengthy.
atoms.feynman: Once you know how the heaviness table changes with joint angles, the fling forces follow automatically.
atoms.visual: Click a cell of M: arrows from it to the Γ cube cells it feeds, with a counter of how many partial derivatives were needed.

atoms.idea: Page 173.

pages.summary: Nonzero Christoffel symbols of the three-link arm, and its gravity vector from link center-of-mass heights via forward kinematics.

atoms.idea: The nonzero Γᵢⱼₖ list: terms in products of sines and cosines of θ2 and θ2+θ3 coupling base spin to shoulder/elbow, and ±l1m3r2 sin θ3 terms coupling shoulder and elbow.
atoms.feynman: Spinning the base flings the arm upward/outward; swinging the shoulder flings the forearm.
atoms.visual: The Γ cube with only the listed cells lit; spin the base and the coral fling torque bars on joints 2 and 3 grow with the matching cells.

atoms.idea: Gravity: N = ∂V/∂θ with V = Σ mᵢghᵢ(θ); heights from forward kinematics are h1 = r0, h2 = l0 − r1 sin θ2, h3 = l0 − l1 sin θ2 − r2 sin(θ2+θ3).
atoms.feynman: Only lifting joints change how high things are; spinning the base never does.
atoms.visual: Slate height rulers on each gold center-of-mass dot; spinning the base leaves them flat, lifting the shoulder moves h2 and h3.

atoms.idea: Page 174.

pages.summary: Gravity vector (4.25) completes Example 4.3; Section 3.3 defines the Lie bracket on se(3) generalizing the cross product, with antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity.

atoms.label: Eq (4.25)
atoms.idea: N = (0, −(m2r1 + m3l1)g cos θ2 − m3gr2 cos(θ2+θ3), −m3gr2 cos(θ2+θ3)), completing the three-link dynamics.
atoms.feynman: The shoulder holds up both arm pieces; the elbow holds up only the forearm.
atoms.visual: Slate gravity torque bars at each joint: zero at the base, biggest at the shoulder, smaller at the elbow; they peak when the arm is horizontal.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.3.3 Robot dynamics and the product of exponentials formula.
For any L = ½θ̇ᵀMθ̇ − V the above holds; with product-of-exponentials kinematics, M and C get explicit formulas in terms of twists.
atoms.feynman: If you build the arm from twist-shaped Lego pieces, the heaviness table can be read straight off the pieces.
atoms.visual: The orange twist axes glow and arrows flow from them into the M and C grids.

atoms.idea: The cross product satisfies (ω1 × ω2)^ = ω̂1ω̂2 − ω̂2ω̂1; by analogy the Lie bracket on se(3) is [ξ̂1, ξ̂2] = ξ̂1ξ̂2 − ξ̂2ξ̂1, again a twist.
atoms.feynman: Turn a book a bit about x, then y, then undo x, then undo y: it ends slightly turned about z. That leftover is the bracket.
atoms.visual: Go-A, go-B, undo-A, undo-B loop on a blue brick using two orange twists; the leftover small motion is drawn as a gold twist arrow and compared with the computed bracket.

atoms.label: Eq (4.26)
atoms.idea: In coordinates: [ξ1, ξ2] = (ξ̂1ξ̂2 − ξ̂2ξ̂1)^∨, a 6-D generalization of the cross product.
atoms.feynman: A cross product for screw motions.
atoms.visual: Two 6-vector twist columns produce a third gold column; restricting both to pure rotations shows it equals ω1 × ω2.

atoms.idea: Properties: antisymmetry [ξ1, ξ2] = −[ξ2, ξ1] and the Jacobi identity; details in Appendix A.
atoms.feynman: Doing the loop in the opposite order leaves the opposite leftover.
atoms.visual: Swap A and B in the loop: the gold leftover arrow flips direction. A triple-loop demo shows the three Jacobi leftovers summing to a zero dot.

atoms.idea: Page 175.

pages.summary: Adjoint chains Aᵢⱼ, link Jacobian columns, base-reflected link inertias M′ᵢ, and Proposition 4.3 giving M and C explicitly from twists.

atoms.label: Eq (4.27)
atoms.idea: Aᵢⱼ is the adjoint of the inverse product of exponentials from joint j+1 to i when i > j, the identity when i = j, and zero when i < j.
atoms.feynman: A relay of translators passing a message from joint j's language to link i's language; nobody downstream talks back upstream.
atoms.visual: A lower-triangular 6×6-block grid: diagonal blocks lime (identity), upper blocks dark (zero), lower blocks animated as chains of Ad hops along the arm.

atoms.idea: The j-th column of link i's body Jacobian is Ad of g_sli(0)⁻¹ applied to Aᵢⱼξⱼ.
atoms.feynman: Each joint's twist, translated hop by hop to link i, then into link i's own frame.
atoms.visual: A teal twist arrow leaves joint j, hops along the links (each hop an Ad), and lands at link i's frame.

atoms.label: Eq (4.28)
atoms.idea: Transformed link inertia M′ᵢ = Adᵀ M ᵢ Ad (with g_sli(0)⁻¹), the link's inertia reflected into the base frame.
atoms.feynman: Describe each piece's heaviness as seen from the base, so all pieces use one language.
atoms.visual: Each link's 6×6 teal block is re-expressed at the base: off-diagonal blocks appear because the base is not at the link's center of mass.

atoms.idea: These definitions give closed-form inertial quantities.
atoms.feynman: Now the recipe can be written in one line.
atoms.visual: Arrows from Aᵢⱼ grid and M′ blocks converge on the M and C grids.

atoms.label: Prop 4.3
atoms.idea: Mᵢⱼ = Σ over l ≥ max(i, j) of ξᵢᵀAₗᵢᵀM′ₗAₗⱼξⱼ, and C from the Christoffel formula, where ∂Mᵢⱼ/∂θₖ is built from Lie brackets [Aₖᵢξᵢ, ξₖ] (4.29)-(4.30).
atoms.feynman: The coupling between joints i and j comes from every link that both of them move, each weighted by its heaviness.
atoms.visual: Click cell Mᵢⱼ: links l ≥ max(i, j) light up and their contributions stack into the cell; clicking a C cell shows gold bracket arrows from the twist-loop picture.

atoms.idea: So all dynamics come from the joint twists, the link reference frames and the link inertias; only the Aᵢⱼ depend on configuration.
atoms.feynman: The ingredients never change; only the angles you turn the joints to do.
atoms.visual: Ingredient tray (twists, frames, inertias) stays frozen while only the Aᵢⱼ grid animates as joints move.

atoms.idea: Page 176.

pages.summary: Proof of Prop 4.3 via ∂(Aₗⱼξⱼ)/∂θₖ = Aₗₖ[Aₖⱼξⱼ, ξₖ]; Example 4.4 idealized SCARA: twists, transformed inertias, and its inertia matrix.

atoms.idea: Key step: write Aᵢⱼ = Ad of a product gᵢⱼ that splits as gᵢₖgₖⱼ; differentiating with respect to θₖ gives ∂(Aₗⱼξⱼ)/∂θₖ = Aₗₖ[Aₖⱼξⱼ, ξₖ] for l ≥ k ≥ j, and zero otherwise; the rest is direct calculation.
atoms.feynman: Wiggling joint k changes how joint j's twist looks downstream exactly by the leftover of a tiny twist-loop between them.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) chain of Ad hops from j to l; (2) wiggle joint k in the middle; (3) the change shows as a gold bracket arrow [Aₖⱼξⱼ, ξₖ]; (4) carried on to l by Aₗₖ. Numeric check: finite-difference arrow overlays the bracket arrow.

atoms.feynman: A pick-and-place arm that swings flat over a table and pokes straight down.

atoms.feynman: A piece far from the base couples pushing and twisting by how far away it is.
atoms.visual: Each link's base-reflected block shows coral off-diagonal blocks whose size grows as you drag pᵢ away from the base.

atoms.idea: Result: 4×4 M(θ) with α + β + 2γ cos θ2 and β + γ cos θ2 couplings in the upper-left, a constant δ block for the wrist, and decoupled m4 for the vertical slide.

atoms.visual: The 4×4 grid: only the cos θ2 cells breathe as the elbow moves; δ cells and m4 stay constant (lime lock icons).

pages.summary: Lyapunov stability survey: the system ẋ = f(x, t), equilibrium points, intuitive local and asymptotic stability (pendulum down vs up), shifting the equilibrium to 0, and Definition 4.1.

atoms.idea: Section 4.4 Lyapunov Stability Theory.
The section surveys, without proofs, the stability tools needed to analyze robot controllers.
atoms.feynman: Before trusting a bridge, learn the tests that tell whether it will sway back or fall.
atoms.visual: A toolbox shelf of three icons (bowl, magnifier, magnet) that open the three stability scenes.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.4.1 Basic definitions.

atoms.label: Eq (4.31)
atoms.idea: System ẋ = f(x, t), x(t0) = x0, with f Lipschitz in x (uniformly in t) and piecewise continuous in t so solutions exist and are unique. x* is an equilibrium if f(x*, t) ≡ 0 for all t.
atoms.feynman: A marble placed exactly at the bottom of a bowl, or exactly balanced on top of an upside-down bowl, stays put: both are resting spots.
atoms.visual: Phase plane with the vector field as small arrows; gold dots mark points where the arrows vanish. Drag a teal start point to see the unique path it follows.

atoms.idea: Informally: stable if solutions starting near x* stay near; asymptotically stable if they also tend to x*. A pendulum hanging down is stable (asymptotically, with damping); pointing up is unstable.
atoms.feynman: A marble in a bowl stays in the bowl; with some sand in the bowl it also comes to rest at the bottom. A marble on top of a dome rolls off.
atoms.visual: Pendulum toggle: hanging down, nudge it and its phase trail circles the gold dot (or spirals in with a damping slider); flip it upright and the trail runs away in coral.

atoms.idea: Shift coordinates so the equilibrium of interest is at the origin; study each equilibrium separately.
atoms.feynman: Move your ruler so the bowl's bottom reads zero.
atoms.visual: Drag the plot's origin onto any gold equilibrium dot; the axes snap there.

atoms.label: Def 4.1
atoms.idea: Lyapunov stability at t0: for every ε > 0 there is δ(t0, ε) > 0 so that |x(t0)| < δ implies |x(t)| < ε for all t ≥ t0 (Eq 4.32).
atoms.feynman: You dare me to keep the marble within any circle I draw; I win if I can always pick a small enough starting circle.
atoms.visual: The ε-δ game: drag a lime ε circle; the scene searches for and draws a smaller teal δ circle; trajectories seeded inside δ (teal) never cross ε. A coral flash if no δ works.

atoms.idea: Lyapunov stability is mild: no convergence required, and it is defined at an initial time t0. Uniform stability asks that δ not depend on t0.
atoms.feynman: Stable only promises the marble won't run away, not that it ever stops; and a promise that doesn't depend on when you start is stronger.
atoms.visual: Undamped pendulum orbit circles forever inside ε (stable, never converges); a time slider for t0 shows δ shrinking for a time-varying example unless uniform.

atoms.idea: Page 179.

pages.summary: Asymptotic and uniform asymptotic stability, instability as the negation of stability, global versus local, uniformity trivial for time-invariant systems, and exponential stability (4.34).

atoms.idea: Continuation: uniform stability means δ works for every starting time.
atoms.feynman: One safety rule that works at any hour of the day.
atoms.visual: The t0 slider moves while the teal δ circle stays the same size (lime lock).

atoms.label: Def 4.2
atoms.idea: Asymptotic stability at t0: stable, and locally attractive: some δ(t0) such that |x(t0)| < δ implies x(t) → 0 (Eq 4.33).
atoms.feynman: Not only does the marble stay in the bowl, it eventually rests at the very bottom.
atoms.visual: Damping slider > 0: trajectories from inside the δ circle spiral into the gold dot; a distance plot falls to zero.

atoms.idea: Uniform asymptotic stability: uniformly stable, uniformly attractive (δ independent of t0), and convergence uniform.
atoms.feynman: However late you start, the marble settles just as fast.
atoms.visual: Several trajectories launched at different t0 from the same point; their distance curves overlap.

atoms.idea: Unstable means not stable (negate the ε-δ statement). For robots we want uniform asymptotic stability: actually reach the target, not just stay near (Fig 4.7).
atoms.feynman: Unstable doesn't need runaway to infinity; it just means some circle can't be guaranteed.
atoms.visual: In the ε-δ game, a saddle field: whatever δ you pick, one teal trajectory escapes the ε circle and flashes coral.

atoms.idea: Definitions are local; global stability holds for all initial conditions. For time-invariant systems stability implies uniform stability.
atoms.feynman: A bowl that catches marbles from anywhere on the table versus only near its rim.
atoms.visual: Drag the start point far away: in a global system it still returns (lime), in a local one it escapes beyond a shaded basin (coral).

atoms.label: Def 4.3
atoms.idea: Exponential stability: constants m, α, ε > 0 with |x(t)| ≤ m e^{−α(t−t0)} |x(t0)| for |x(t0)| ≤ ε (Eq 4.34).
atoms.feynman: Every second, the marble's distance from the bottom shrinks at least by a fixed fraction, like a bouncing ball losing a set share each bounce.
atoms.visual: Distance-vs-time log plot: a gold envelope line m e^{−αt}; the teal distance curve always stays under it. An α slider tightens the envelope until it is violated.

atoms.idea: Page 180.

pages.summary: Phase portraits (stable, asymptotically stable, saddle), rate of convergence and strength of exponential stability; the direct method of Lyapunov introduced via energy.

atoms.label: Fig 4.7
atoms.idea: Three phase portraits: (a) closed orbits around the origin (stable but not attracting), (b) spirals into the origin (asymptotically stable), (c) a saddle (unstable).
atoms.feynman: A frictionless swing loops forever; a real swing slows to a stop; a ball on a saddle rolls off one side.
atoms.visual: Three tiles of phase planes with streaming teal particles: ellipses, inward spirals, and a saddle with two coral escape lines.

atoms.idea: The largest α allowed in (4.34) is the rate of convergence.
atoms.feynman: How fast the ball loses its bounce.
atoms.visual: The α slider readout stops at the largest value that still bounds the curve; that number is labeled with a gold α.

atoms.idea: Exponential stability implies uniform asymptotic stability, is robust to perturbations, and is needed for advanced (e.g. adaptive) control; global exponential stability is the goal.
atoms.feynman: A ball that loses half its bounce every time is robust: a tiny extra tap barely matters.
atoms.visual: Add a small coral disturbance push: the exponential system stays inside a thin tube around zero, while a slower-than-exponential one drifts.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.4.2 The direct method of Lyapunov.
The direct (second) method decides stability without solving the ODE, by checking how an energy-like function changes along trajectories.
atoms.feynman: You can tell a ball will settle in a bowl without tracking it: just notice it keeps losing height-plus-speed energy.
atoms.visual: A blue bowl surface V over the phase plane; a ball rides its trajectory on the bowl; an energy bar beside it only ticks downward.

atoms.idea: Page 181.

pages.summary: Locally positive definite, positive definite and decrescent functions; V̇ along trajectories; Theorem 4.4 parts 1–2 (stability, uniform stability).

atoms.label: Def 4.4
atoms.idea: With B_ε the ε-ball, V is locally positive definite if V(0, t) = 0 and V(x, t) ≥ α(|x|) on B_ε for a strictly increasing α: locally an energy (Eq 4.35).
atoms.feynman: A bowl: zero at the bottom and rising in every direction, at least as steep as some fixed cup.
atoms.visual: Blue bowl V with a fixed gold cup α(|x|) underneath; morph V over time: it may wiggle but never dips below the gold cup.

atoms.label: Def 4.5
atoms.idea: Positive definite: also α(p) → ∞ as p → ∞ (globally energy-like).
atoms.feynman: A bowl whose walls keep rising forever, so no marble can escape over a rim.
atoms.visual: Zoom out: a pdf bowl keeps rising; a merely lpdf one flattens at the rim and a coral marble rolls out over it.

atoms.label: Def 4.6
atoms.idea: Decrescent: V(x, t) ≤ β(|x|) for a strictly increasing β; an upper cup bounds V uniformly in time (Eq 4.36).
atoms.feynman: The bowl may change shape over time, but never grows taller than a fixed outer bowl.
atoms.visual: A second, lime outer cup β above V; time-varying V stays sandwiched between gold α and lime β.

atoms.idea: V̇ along trajectories: ∂V/∂t + (∂V/∂x) f.
atoms.feynman: How fast your height changes as you walk = slope under your feet × your walking velocity (plus the hill moving).
atoms.visual: At the ball's position: a teal f arrow and the gradient of V; their dot product is a bar that is negative (lime) when the arrow points downhill.

atoms.label: Thm 4.4 (1-2)
atoms.idea: If V is lpdf and V̇ ≤ 0 locally, the origin is stable; if V is also decrescent, uniformly stable.
atoms.feynman: If the marble can never gain energy, it can never climb out of a bowl: it stays near the bottom.
atoms.visual: Proof staircase: (1) pick ε, draw its circle; (2) find the lowest bowl height on that circle, a gold level line; (3) choose δ so starting energy is below it; (4) the energy bar never rises, so the ball can never reach the circle. Lime check.

atoms.idea: Page 182.

pages.summary: Table 4.1 and Theorem 4.4 parts 3–4 (uniform asymptotic and global stability); sufficiency and converse theorems; Theorem 4.5 for exponential stability via quadratic bounds.

atoms.label: Table 4.1
atoms.idea: Summary: lpdf + (−V̇ ≥ 0) → stable; add decrescent → uniformly stable; −V̇ lpdf → uniformly asymptotically stable; pdf, decrescent, −V̇ pdf → globally uniformly asymptotically stable.
atoms.feynman: The better your bowl and the more strictly energy drops, the stronger the promise.
atoms.visual: A 4-row ladder of bowl icons; toggling checkboxes (lpdf, decrescent, −V̇ lpdf, pdf) climbs the ladder and the conclusion badge upgrades.

atoms.label: Thm 4.4 (3-4)
atoms.idea: If V is lpdf and decrescent and −V̇ is lpdf, the origin is uniformly locally asymptotically stable; with pdf versions everywhere, globally.
atoms.feynman: If the marble always loses some energy whenever it isn't at the bottom, it must eventually reach the bottom.
atoms.visual: Damped bowl: the energy bar strictly falls whenever the ball is off-center; the ball reaches the gold bottom. Global toggle: start anywhere on an unbounded bowl and it still comes home.

atoms.idea: Thm 4.4 is only sufficient and gives no recipe for V; converse theorems guarantee a V exists when the point is stable, but don't say how to compute it.
atoms.feynman: Finding the right bowl is an art: a bad guess proves nothing, though a good bowl always exists for a stable marble.
atoms.visual: Draw-your-own V: the learner sculpts bowl level sets; trajectories crossing a level set outward flash coral (bad V), all inward lime (good V).

atoms.idea: Thm 4.4 gives no rates; it can be strengthened for exponential stability.
atoms.feynman: Knowing the ball stops isn't knowing when.
atoms.visual: A stopwatch icon appears beside the energy bar.

atoms.label: Thm 4.5
atoms.idea: Exponential stability iff there is V with α1|x|² ≤ V ≤ α2|x|², V̇ ≤ −α3|x|², and |∂V/∂x| ≤ α4|x| near 0.
atoms.feynman: If energy is boxed between two quadratic bowls and always drains at a quadratic rate, it shrinks by a fixed fraction per second.
atoms.visual: V drawn between two gold parabolas α1|x|², α2|x|²; the V̇ bar stays below −α3|x|² (coral line); the log-distance plot becomes a straight descending line.

atoms.idea: Page 183.

pages.summary: Exponential rate bounds from Theorem 4.5; the indirect method: Jacobian linearization A(t), uniform remainder condition, and Theorem 4.6 stability by linearization.

atoms.idea: Rate bounds: m ≤ (α2/α1)^{1/2} and α ≥ α3/(2α2); global if the bounds hold everywhere.
atoms.feynman: A steep bowl that drains fast gives a fast guaranteed rate; a lopsided bowl makes the guarantee looser.
atoms.visual: Sliders for α1, α2, α3 move the gold envelope m e^{−αt} on the distance plot live.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.4.3 The indirect method of Lyapunov.

atoms.label: Eq (4.37)-(4.39)
atoms.idea: For ẋ = f(x, t) with f(0, t) = 0, let A(t) = ∂f/∂x at 0 and f1 = f − A x. Require the remainder to vanish faster than |x|, uniformly in t.
atoms.feynman: Zoom far enough into any smooth curve and it looks like a straight line.
atoms.visual: Magnifier over the gold equilibrium: as zoom grows, curved field arrows straighten into the linear field Ax; a coral remainder bar f1/|x| shrinks to zero.

atoms.label: Eq (4.40)
atoms.idea: Then ż = A(t)z is the uniform linearization; its stability decides local stability of the nonlinear system.
atoms.feynman: Testing a tiny model of the bowl's bottom tells you about the real bowl near its bottom.
atoms.visual: Side-by-side: real nonlinear phase portrait and its linear stand-in, identical near the center.

atoms.label: Thm 4.6
atoms.idea: If the remainder condition holds, A is bounded, and 0 is uniformly asymptotically stable for the linearization, then 0 is locally uniformly asymptotically stable for the nonlinear system.
atoms.feynman: If the straight-line zoom says 'rolls to center', the real thing does too, at least near the center.
atoms.visual: Lime badge on the linear tile copies over to the nonlinear tile, inside a shaded neighborhood circle only.

atoms.idea: Page 184.

pages.summary: Damped oscillator figure; counterexamples without uniform asymptotic stability; eigenvalue test for time-invariant systems; domain of attraction; Example 4.5 begins.

atoms.label: Fig 4.8
atoms.idea: Damped harmonic oscillator: mass M, spring K, damper B, position q.
atoms.feynman: A screen door with a spring closer and an air damper.
atoms.visual: Blue block on a slate floor, orange coil spring K to a wall, teal dashpot B, position slider q.

atoms.idea: The theorem needs uniform asymptotic stability of the linearization; without it counterexamples exist.
atoms.feynman: If the zoomed model only balances on a knife-edge, the real system's small curves decide.
atoms.visual: Purple eigenvalue on the imaginary axis: the linear tile shows closed orbits while two nonlinear tiles beside it spiral in (lime) and out (coral).

atoms.idea: Time-invariant case: if all eigenvalues of A = ∂f/∂x at 0 have negative real parts, the origin is asymptotically stable.
atoms.feynman: If every natural motion of the zoomed model decays, the system settles.
atoms.visual: Complex-plane panel: eigenvalue dots; drag a parameter; when all are in the lime left half plane the badge reads stable, any in the coral right half reads unstable.

atoms.idea: Linearization only gives a local result; estimating the region of attraction is a research problem tied to finding good Lyapunov functions.
atoms.feynman: The zoom tells you a marble near the bottom returns, not how big the bowl is.
atoms.visual: Grid of starting points colored lime (returns) or coral (escapes) shows the true basin; a conservative ellipse from a quadratic V sits inside it.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.4.4 Examples.
The stability theorems are now applied to examples.
atoms.feynman: Try the tests on real toys.
atoms.visual: Example tabs appear: oscillator, nonlinear spring.

atoms.label: Ex 4.5
atoms.idea: Linear damped oscillator: M q̈ + B q̇ + K q = 0 with M, B, K > 0 (Eq 4.41).
atoms.feynman: A door closer: spring pulls it shut, damper keeps it from slamming.
atoms.visual: The block-spring-damper oscillates when released; M, B, K sliders.

atoms.idea: Page 185.

pages.summary: Oscillator poles show global exponential stability; energy as Lyapunov function gives only V̇ = −Bq̇², which is not negative definite because level sets are tangent to the flow; a skewed energy fixes this.

atoms.label: Eq (4.42)
atoms.idea: State form with x = (q, q̇): d/dt(q, q̇) = (q̇, −(K/M)q − (B/M)q̇).
atoms.feynman: Track both where the door is and how fast it is moving.
atoms.visual: Phase plane axes q and q̇; the block's state is a teal dot moving along its trajectory.

atoms.idea: A = [[0, 1], [−K/M, −B/M]], characteristic equation λ² + (B/M)λ + K/M = 0, roots (−B ± √(B² − 4KM))/(2M) always in the left half plane: globally exponentially stable.
atoms.feynman: However you set a real spring and damper, the door always stops.
atoms.visual: Complex-plane dots for the two roots move with B and K sliders; they stay lime in the left half, merging on the real axis at critical damping.

atoms.label: Eq (4.43)-(4.44)
atoms.idea: Try energy V = ½Mq̇² + ½Kq²: V̇ = −Bq̇², which vanishes whenever q̇ = 0 regardless of q, so −V̇ is not positive definite; only LaSalle could give asymptotic stability, which is too weak here.
atoms.feynman: At the moment the door stops to turn around, it isn't losing any energy at all, even though it's not shut.
atoms.visual: Energy bowl with the teal state dot; the energy bar shows flat steps each time the trajectory crosses the q̇ = 0 axis (purple stripe), proving V̇ is only ≤ 0.

atoms.idea: Why it fails (Fig 4.9a): energy level sets are tangent to the flow on q̇ = 0.
atoms.feynman: Rolling along a contour line for a moment means no height lost.
atoms.visual: Ellipse level sets overlaid on the flow; at q̇ = 0 the flow arrows lie along the ellipses, highlighted purple.

atoms.idea: Skew the level sets: V = ½q̇Mq̇ + ½qKq + ε q̇Mq, the quadratic form with matrix [[K, εM], [εM, M]].
atoms.feynman: Tilt the bowl a little so the marble always crosses the contour lines downhill.
atoms.visual: An ε slider rotates the elliptical level sets slightly; tangency points vanish and every crossing arrow is inward (lime).

atoms.idea: Page 186.

pages.summary: Energy vs skewed level sets figure; the skewed V̇ is negative definite for small ε, giving exponential stability; Example 4.6 nonlinear spring-damper with passive f, g.

atoms.label: Fig 4.9
atoms.idea: Oscillator flow with level sets of (a) the plain energy, tangent on q̇ = 0, and (b) the skewed energy, crossed transversally everywhere.
atoms.feynman: Contour lines on a hill: in (b) every path always walks downhill across them.
atoms.visual: Two tiles of teal flow lines with dashed blue level sets; tangency spots purple in (a), none in (b).

atoms.idea: V̇ = (−B + εM)q̇² + ε(−Kq² − Bqq̇) = −xᵀQx with Q = [[εK, εB/2], [εB/2, B − εM]], positive definite for small ε (Exercise 11): exponential stability.
atoms.feynman: A slight tilt costs a tiny bit of the damper's drain but now drains energy everywhere, not just when moving.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) V̇ bar split into damper and tilt parts; (2) Q matrix as an ellipse; (3) raise ε until the ellipse would flatten (coral); (4) small ε keeps it lime: V̇ < 0 except at the origin, and the log-distance plot is a straight line.

atoms.idea: The same skewing trick is used for the robot controller proofs that follow.
atoms.feynman: We'll tilt the arm's energy bowl the same way.
atoms.visual: Arrow linking this tile to the PD-control scene's energy bowl.

atoms.label: Ex 4.6
atoms.idea: Unit mass, nonlinear spring g and damper f: ẋ1 = x2, ẋ2 = −f(x2) − g(x1) (Eq 4.45), with passive f, g: σf(σ) ≥ 0 and σg(σ) ≥ 0 near 0, equality only at 0.
atoms.feynman: A weird spring and sticky damper still always push back toward rest and never push you along.
atoms.visual: Draw-your-own f and g curves in small panels; they must sit in the lime quadrants (same sign as σ); then the block simulates.

atoms.idea: Page 187.

pages.summary: Nonlinear spring Lyapunov function gives only stability; LaSalle's principle: ω-limit sets, invariant sets, and the theorem statement begins.

atoms.idea: Take V = x2²/2 + ∫₀^{x1} g; passivity of g makes V lpdf, and V̇ = −x2 f(x2) ≤ 0: stability but not yet asymptotic stability, which needs LaSalle.
atoms.feynman: Motion energy plus spring energy never goes up because the damper only eats energy, but it eats nothing at the turnaround moments.
atoms.visual: Bowl built from the drawn g curve; energy bar only falls, with flat steps whenever x2 = 0 (purple stripe).

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.4.5 Lasalle's invariance principle.
LaSalle gives asymptotic stability even when −V̇ is not lpdf, for autonomous (or periodic) systems ẋ = f(x) with solutions s(t, x0, t0) (Eq 4.46).
atoms.feynman: If energy stops dropping only in places where you can't stay, you must keep dropping until you reach a place you can stay.
atoms.visual: The purple V̇ = 0 stripe glows; balls landing on it immediately slide off it, except at the gold origin.

atoms.label: Def 4.7
atoms.idea: ω-limit set: points y that the trajectory comes arbitrarily close to at an increasing sequence of times going to infinity.
atoms.feynman: Where a wandering ant keeps coming back to, again and again, forever.
atoms.visual: A trajectory leaves a fading trail; late-time trail segments are drawn gold and accumulate into a point or a loop: the ω-limit set.

atoms.label: Def 4.8
atoms.idea: Positively invariant set M: trajectories that start in M stay in M for all later time.
atoms.feynman: A fenced garden with gates that only open inward.
atoms.visual: Lime region; seed teal particles inside; none ever leave. Drag the region's boundary: if any particle escapes it turns coral.

atoms.idea: Every ω-limit set is closed and invariant.
atoms.feynman: Where the ant ends up circling is itself a place it never leaves.
atoms.visual: The gold ω-limit loop is shown also glowing lime (invariant).

atoms.label: Thm 4.7
atoms.idea: LaSalle: let V be lpdf with V̇ ≤ 0 on the compact sublevel set Ω_c = {V ≤ c}; define S = {x ∈ Ω_c : V̇ = 0}.
atoms.feynman: Inside the bowl up to a certain height, energy never rises; mark the spots where it doesn't fall.
atoms.visual: Ω_c drawn as a blue filled sublevel region; inside it the teal S stripe where V̇ = 0.

atoms.idea: Page 188.

pages.summary: LaSalle's conclusion: trajectories tend to the largest invariant set in S; Example 4.7 proves asymptotic stability of the nonlinear spring-damper; limits for nonperiodic systems; Section 5 position control begins.

atoms.idea: Conclusion: trajectories approach the largest invariant set inside S; if that set is just {0}, the origin is asymptotically stable.
atoms.feynman: If the only place on the 'not losing energy' stripe where you can stay forever is the bottom, you end at the bottom.
atoms.visual: Within the teal S stripe, a search animation tests each point: start there, does it stay in S? Only the gold origin passes (lime); all others flash coral and slide off.

atoms.idea: A global version exists too.
atoms.feynman: Works for the whole table if the bowl is big enough.
atoms.visual: Ω_c slider extended to the whole plane.

atoms.label: Ex 4.7
atoms.idea: Nonlinear spring again: choose c so V̇ ≤ 0 on Ω_c; S is Ω_c ∩ {x2 = 0}. Staying in S forces x1 constant and then g(x10) = 0, so x10 = 0: the origin is locally asymptotically stable.
atoms.feynman: A stopped block with a stretched spring can't stay stopped: the spring yanks it. Only the unstretched, stopped block stays.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) Ω_c region; (2) stripe x2 = 0; (3) place a block stopped at x1 ≠ 0, spring arrow (orange) pulls it off the stripe (coral); (4) only x1 = 0 stays; (5) all trajectories spiral to the gold origin.

atoms.idea: LaSalle extends to periodic systems but not to general time-varying ones, limiting its use.
atoms.feynman: The trick needs the rules of the game not to change over time.
atoms.visual: A time-varying toggle greys out the LaSalle magnet icon.

atoms.idea: Section 4.5 Position Control and Trajectory Tracking.
Problem: choose joint torques so the arm follows a desired trajectory robustly to initial errors, noise and model error, assuming ideal torque actuators.
atoms.feynman: Steer a cart along a painted line even though it starts off the line, the floor is bumpy, and you don't know its exact weight.
atoms.visual: A gold path for the arm's joints; the blue arm starts off it; perturbation sliders (initial error, noise, mass error) are ready.
