pages.summary: Tracking problem for M θ̈ + Cθ̇ + N = τ; open-loop torques along θd work only with perfect model and initial conditions; feedback is required; controllers rely only on Lemma 4.2 properties; computed torque begins.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.5.1 Problem description.

atoms.label: Eq (4.47)
atoms.idea: Given the arm dynamics M θ̈ + Cθ̇ + N = τ and a twice-differentiable desired joint trajectory θd(t), choose τ to track it.
atoms.feynman: A dance routine written as a timeline of poses; the dancer must hit each pose on time.
atoms.visual: A gold ghost arm sweeps θd(t) along a gold path in joint space; a time scrubber; the blue real arm waits for torques.

atoms.idea: Open loop: τ = M(θd)θ̈d + C(θd, θ̇d)θ̇d + N(θd, θ̇d). With a perfect model and matching initial state, uniqueness of ODE solutions gives θ = θd exactly.
atoms.feynman: Replaying a recorded set of pushes on a swing works only if the swing starts exactly where it did in the recording.
atoms.visual: Play the precomputed torque tape: with matching start the blue arm overlays the gold ghost perfectly; the robot's own state is not used (no feedback wire drawn).

atoms.idea: Open loop is fragile: any initial error is never corrected and nearby starts need not stay nearby. Feedback must make the actual trajectory converge; for a setpoint, closed loop must be asymptotically stable.
atoms.feynman: Walking a line blindfolded: start a step off and you never find it again.
atoms.visual: Nudge the blue arm's start: the coral error between blue and gold persists or grows under the tape. A feedback wire icon is then connected and the error shrinks.

atoms.idea: The controllers are proved using only the structural properties of Lemma 4.2, so they apply to every open-chain arm; actual performance still depends on the arm and is a starting point for tuning.
atoms.feynman: A rule that works for every swing because it only uses facts true of all swings.
atoms.visual: Swap arm models (two-link, three-link, SCARA) under the same controller: the lime convergence badge stays; the settling time readout differs.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.5.2 Computed torque.
Refinement: use the measured state to cancel all nonlinearities and supply exactly the torque needed for the desired acceleration.
atoms.feynman: Hold the shopping cart steady against every slope and bump, then push it exactly as much as you want it to speed up.
atoms.visual: Measured θ, θ̇ flow (teal wires) into the model block.

atoms.idea: Page 190.

pages.summary: Cancelling nonlinearities gives θ̈ = θ̈d; adding PD feedback on the error gives linear error dynamics ë + Kvė + Kpe = 0; the law splits into feedforward and feedback.

atoms.label: Eq (4.48)
atoms.idea: τ = M(θ)θ̈d + C(θ, θ̇)θ̇ + N(θ, θ̇) gives M θ̈ = M θ̈d, so θ̈ = θ̈d since M is positive definite; still no correction of initial errors.
atoms.feynman: Cancel every hill and wind for a cyclist, and she accelerates exactly as commanded, but if she started in the wrong lane she stays in it.
atoms.visual: Blue arm under full cancellation: acceleration arrows match the gold ghost's exactly; a start offset keeps a constant coral gap.

atoms.label: Eq (4.49)-(4.50)
atoms.idea: Computed torque law: τ = M(θ)(θ̈d − Kvė − Kpe) + Cθ̇ + N with e = θ − θd, giving error dynamics M(ë + Kvė + Kpe) = 0, hence ë + Kvė + Kpe = 0.
atoms.feynman: After cancelling everything, attach a virtual spring and damper from the arm to its ghost; the error then behaves like a plain spring-damper.
atoms.visual: Error plot: the coral error decays like a mass-spring-damper; Kp and Kv sliders change the decay, and the pole dots in the complex plane move accordingly.

atoms.idea: Split: τ = τff + τfb with τff = Mθ̈d + Cθ̇ + N driving the nominal path and τfb = M(−Kvė − Kpe) correcting errors.
atoms.feynman: Feedforward is the planned push; feedback is the correction when you see you're off.
atoms.visual: Stacked torque bar per joint: blue feedforward segment and orange feedback segment; with zero error the orange part vanishes.

atoms.idea: Because the error equation is linear, Kv and Kp are easy to choose for exponential convergence.
atoms.feynman: Tuning a plain spring-damper is a solved problem.
atoms.visual: Pole-placement drag: pull the pole dots left; error curve gets faster.

atoms.idea: Page 191.

pages.summary: Diagonal gains decouple joints; Proposition 4.8 (positive definite gains give exponential tracking) with an eigenvalue proof; computed torque as feedback linearization and its practicality.

atoms.idea: Diagonal Kp, Kv give independent, decoupled exponentially stable error loops per joint.
atoms.feynman: Each joint gets its own private spring-damper that ignores the others.
atoms.visual: Per-joint error plots evolve independently; changing joint 1's gains never alters joint 2's curve.

atoms.label: Prop 4.8
atoms.idea: If Kp and Kv are symmetric positive definite, computed torque gives exponential trajectory tracking.
atoms.feynman: Any real spring and real damper (positive in every direction) make the error die out exponentially.
atoms.visual: Gain matrices shown as lime ellipses (positive definite); the log-error plot becomes a straight falling line. Making a gain ellipse flat or inverted flashes coral.

atoms.idea: Write the error as a linear system with A = [[0, I], [−Kp, −Kv]]. For an eigenpair (λ, v), λ = 0 is impossible, v1 ≠ 0; normalizing v1 gives λ² + αλ + β = 0 with α = v1*Kvv1 > 0, β = v1*Kpv1 > 0, so Re λ < 0.
atoms.feynman: Every natural motion of the error is a little spring-damper with positive stiffness and damping, and those always die out.
atoms.visual: Staircase: (1) the block matrix A; (2) pick an eigenvector, show v2 = λv1; (3) squeeze it into a scalar quadratic with gold α, β bars, both positive; (4) the roots land in the lime left half-plane.

atoms.idea: Computed torque is feedback linearization: nonlinear state feedback makes the system linear so linear design tools apply. It can be computation- and torque-hungry in general, but for arms M is bounded so torques stay bounded, and it performs well in practice.
atoms.feynman: Wearing glasses that straighten a warped world so you can use a ruler.
atoms.visual: Toggle 'linearizing glasses': the twisted nonlinear closed-loop phase portrait becomes the clean linear one, and a torque-magnitude meter stays within a lime bound. Where the glasses crack: a model-mismatch slider scales the arm's masses, the error stops obeying the linear law and a coral residual remains.

atoms.idea: Page 192.

pages.summary: PD control τ = −Kvė − Kpe from linear design; Proposition 4.9 global asymptotic setpoint stability with the energy Lyapunov function, using Ṁ − 2C skew to get V̇ = −θ̇ᵀKvθ̇.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.5.3 PD control.
Alternative design: a linear controller based on linearization is locally stable, and often global stability can be shown with an explicit Lyapunov function.
atoms.feynman: A simple rule designed for the middle of the room might still work everywhere if you can prove it.
atoms.visual: Local lime basin around the target expands to the whole plane once a Lyapunov bowl is found.

atoms.label: Eq (4.51)
atoms.idea: PD law: τ = −Kvė − Kpe with positive definite gains. No feedforward, so exact tracking of moving targets is impossible; integral action can remove steady error but risks instability and windup.
atoms.feynman: Tie each joint to its target with a spring and a shock absorber.
atoms.visual: Orange coil springs from each joint to a gold setpoint marker and teal dashpots; a moving gold target leaves a persistent coral lag.

atoms.label: Prop 4.9
atoms.idea: For a fixed setpoint and Kv, Kp > 0, PD makes θ = θd globally asymptotically stable (gravity absent or compensated).
atoms.feynman: Springs plus friction always bring a released arm to rest at the spring's center.
atoms.visual: Drop the arm from any pose: it swings and settles exactly at the gold target.

atoms.label: Eq (4.52)
atoms.idea: Closed loop M θ̈ + Cθ̇ + Kvθ̇ + Kpθ = 0 (θd = 0). V = ½θ̇ᵀMθ̇ + ½θᵀKpθ (pdf, decrescent). V̇ = −θ̇ᵀKvθ̇ + ½θ̇ᵀ(Ṁ − 2C)θ̇ = −θ̇ᵀKvθ̇ by skew symmetry.
atoms.feynman: The arm's motion energy plus spring energy can only leak out through the shock absorbers.
atoms.visual: Energy staircase: (1) blue T plus orange spring bar = V; (2) V̇ splits into a teal damper drain and a coral Ṁ−2C bar; (3) the coral bar is shown identically zero; (4) the V bar falls exactly at the damper's rate.

atoms.idea: Page 193.

pages.summary: LaSalle completes Prop 4.9 (only θ = 0 is invariant in θ̇ = 0); augmented PD law with feedforward and Cθ̇d; Proposition 4.10 exponential tracking, proof begins with a skewed energy.

atoms.idea: V̇ = −θ̇ᵀKvθ̇ is only semidefinite (zero whenever θ̇ = 0), so Thm 4.4 alone gives stability.
atoms.feynman: At the top of each swing, the shock absorber isn't working.
atoms.visual: V bar has flat steps each time the arm momentarily stops (purple flashes).

atoms.idea: LaSalle: S = {θ̇ = 0}; staying there forces Kpθ = 0, so θ = 0 is the only invariant set: asymptotic stability.
atoms.feynman: A stopped arm still pulled by a stretched spring cannot stay stopped; only the relaxed pose is a resting place.
atoms.visual: Freeze the arm at a non-target pose with θ̇ = 0: orange spring arrows immediately pull it off the stripe (coral); only at the gold target do the arrows vanish (lime).

atoms.label: Eq (4.53)
atoms.idea: Augmented PD: τ = M(θ)θ̈d + C(θ, θ̇)θ̇d + N − Kvė − Kpe; note Cθ̇d (not Cθ̇), chosen to make the proof work.
atoms.feynman: Add the planned push for the moving target, plus the spring-damper for corrections.
atoms.visual: Torque bar per joint: blue feedforward (with θ̇d-labeled Coriolis piece) plus orange PD feedback; gold target now moves.

atoms.label: Prop 4.10
atoms.idea: With Kv, Kp > 0 the augmented PD law gives exponential trajectory tracking.
atoms.feynman: Springs riding along with a moving target, plus the planned pushes, keep you locked on.
atoms.visual: The blue arm tracks a moving gold ghost; log-error plot is a falling line.

atoms.label: Eq (4.54)
atoms.idea: Closed loop M ë + C ė + Kvė + Kpe = 0. Energy gives only semidefinite V̇ and the system is time-varying (no LaSalle), so use the skewed V = ½ėᵀMė + ½eᵀKpe + ε eᵀMė.
atoms.feynman: Same trick as the door closer: tilt the bowl so energy drains even at the turnaround points.
atoms.visual: The tilted bowl from the oscillator scene reappears over the arm's error plane; ε slider rotates its level sets.

atoms.idea: Page 194.

pages.summary: Skewed V̇ is negative definite for small ε (exponential tracking); modeling errors cause tracking errors; gains chosen from linearization mid-workspace; workspace control introduced via inverse kinematics and its drawbacks.

atoms.idea: Using Ṁ − 2C skew, V̇ = −ėᵀ(Kv − εM)ė − εeᵀKpe + εeᵀ(−Kv + ½Ṁ)ė, which is negative definite for small ε (Exercise 11): exponential stability by Thm 4.5.
atoms.feynman: A slight tilt keeps the damper's drain and adds a small drain from the spring, enough to drain everywhere.
atoms.visual: V̇ quadratic form drawn as an ellipse in (e, ė); raising ε too far flattens it coral; small ε keeps it lime. The log-error line confirms a fixed rate.

atoms.idea: For a setpoint, the augmented law reduces to PD. Exact tracking needs exact models of friction, gravity and inertia; modeling errors produce tracking errors.
atoms.feynman: Pre-planned pushes only help if you know the arm's weight.
atoms.visual: Mismatch slider on mass and gravity: a steady coral tracking residual appears and grows with the mismatch.

atoms.idea: Gain selection: linearize about θ0 to get M(θ0)ë + Kvė + Kpe = 0 and design with linear tools; along a trajectory this may not hold, so in practice gains are picked around a mid-workspace pose.
atoms.feynman: Tune a car's suspension on an average road and hope it is fine elsewhere.
atoms.visual: Tune at a mid pose and watch the response quality badge as the arm moves to a stretched pose: damping ratio readout drifts.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.5.4 Workspace control.
Given a desired end-effector path gd(t) ∈ SE(3), one could solve inverse kinematics at each instant for θd(t) and use joint-space control.
atoms.feynman: Turn a drawing of where the hand should go into instructions for each joint, then follow those.
atoms.visual: Pink hand target path in gold; an IK solver converts it into joint ghost angles each frame (orange dials).

atoms.idea: Drawbacks begin: inverse kinematics is expensive in real time.
atoms.feynman: Translating every instruction on the fly is slow.
atoms.visual: A compute-time meter for the IK step fills each frame.

atoms.idea: Page 195.

pages.summary: Joint-space gains give straight lines in θ but curved hand paths; workspace control writes dynamics in end-effector coordinates x = f(θ) with n = p, via ẋ = Jθ̇.

atoms.idea: Joint-space gains are hard to relate to the task; diagonal computed torque gives straight lines in θ but curved paths of the hand in SE(3).
atoms.feynman: Moving each joint at a steady pace makes your fingertip trace an arc, not the straight line you wanted.
atoms.visual: Command a step: orange joint-space trail is straight in the θ1-θ2 plot while the pink hand trail curves in the workspace.

atoms.idea: Instead write the controller directly in end-effector coordinates x, avoiding inverse kinematics and giving task-meaningful gains, at the cost of local coordinates for SE(3) (e.g. Euler angles).
atoms.feynman: Steer by watching the pen tip rather than your knuckles.
atoms.visual: The knob moves to the pink hand: drag the gold target and gains now appear as springs on the hand itself.

atoms.idea: Let f: Q → Rᵖ be smooth and invertible from joints to workspace variables, so n = p; p < 6 allowed, e.g. SCARA position plus yaw.
atoms.feynman: One knob per thing you care about: as many joints as hand coordinates.
atoms.visual: Arm with n orange joint dials and p pink hand readouts; a counter shows n = p (lime) or mismatch (coral).

atoms.idea: Start from joint dynamics M θ̈ + Cθ̇ + N = τ.
atoms.feynman: The arm's usual rulebook.
atoms.visual: The four-bar torque balance from the arm scene sits in a corner.

atoms.idea: With J = ∂f/∂θ (not the manipulator Jacobian), ẋ = Jθ̇, so θ̇ = J⁻¹ẋ and θ̈ = J⁻¹ẍ + d/dt(J⁻¹)ẋ.
atoms.feynman: Convert hand speed to joint speed by running the gearbox backwards.
atoms.visual: Drag a pink hand velocity arrow; orange joint-speed dials respond via J⁻¹; near a singular pose they spin wildly (🚫 flash).

atoms.idea: Page 196.

pages.summary: Workspace dynamics M̃ẍ + C̃ẋ + Ñ = F with M̃ = J⁻ᵀMJ⁻¹ etc., interpreted as Lagrange's equations in x; Lemma 4.11 keeps symmetry/positivity and skew-symmetry.

atoms.idea: Substitute into the dynamics and premultiply by J⁻ᵀ.
atoms.feynman: Rewrite the arm's rulebook in the hand's language.
atoms.visual: Joint-space torque bars morph through a J⁻ᵀ lens into hand-space force arrows.

atoms.label: Eq (4.55)
atoms.idea: Effective parameters: M̃ = J⁻ᵀMJ⁻¹, C̃ = J⁻ᵀ(CJ⁻¹ + M d/dt J⁻¹), Ñ = J⁻ᵀN, F = J⁻ᵀτ; dynamics M̃ẍ + C̃ẋ + Ñ = F.
atoms.feynman: How heavy the hand feels when you push it depends on the direction and the arm's pose.
atoms.visual: Hand inertia ellipse M̃ drawn blue at the pink hand; push the hand with a teal force and its acceleration follows the ellipse's axes, not the push direction.

atoms.idea: M̃, C̃, Ñ describe the arm seen from the workspace; eliminating θ shows this is Lagrange's equations in coordinates x, though θ is kept since it is what is measured.
atoms.feynman: Same arm, different choice of knobs; the physics rule is the same.
atoms.visual: Toggle generalized coordinates θ ↔ x: the same blue arm motion, the four torque bars re-expressed as hand forces.

atoms.idea: To reuse the controller proofs, the workspace dynamics must keep the structural properties.
atoms.feynman: Check the new rulebook still has the safety features.
atoms.visual: Checkmarks pending beside 'M̃ symmetric positive' and 'skew' badges.

atoms.label: Lemma 4.11
atoms.idea: M̃ is symmetric positive definite and dM̃/dt − 2C̃ is skew-symmetric.
atoms.feynman: The hand still feels some heaviness in every direction and the fling forces still don't create energy.
atoms.visual: M̃ ellipse always lime (fat); a power meter ẋᵀ(dM̃/dt − 2C̃)ẋ pinned at zero.

atoms.idea: Property 1 from J invertible; property 2 by rewriting dM̃/dt − 2C̃ as J⁻ᵀ(Ṁ − 2C)J⁻¹ plus terms in d/dt J⁻¹ that cancel antisymmetrically.
atoms.feynman: Squeezing a skew trade through the same lens on both sides keeps it a fair trade.
atoms.visual: Staircase: Ṁ − 2C mirror-pair grid sandwiched by J⁻ᵀ and J⁻¹ stays mirror-paired; the extra d/dt(J⁻¹) terms appear as a canceling pair.

atoms.idea: Page 197.

pages.summary: Workspace computed torque F = M̃(ẍd − Kvė − Kpe) + C̃ẋ + Ñ, τ = JᵀF; gains in task terms, no inverse kinematics; M̃ blows up near singularities; Example 4.8 compares joint and workspace step responses.

atoms.idea: Direct calculation confirms skew symmetry.
atoms.feynman: The fair-trade check passes.
atoms.visual: Lime check appears on the skew badge.

atoms.idea: Workspace computed torque: F = M̃(ẍd − Kvė − Kpe) + C̃ẋ + Ñ, τ = JᵀF, e = x − xd; error dynamics ë + Kvė + Kpe = 0 as before. PD extends similarly.
atoms.feynman: Put the virtual spring-damper on the hand itself, pulling it to the moving target.
atoms.visual: Orange spring and teal damper attached between pink hand and gold target; hand force F mapped to joint torques by Jᵀ (orange bars); the coral hand error decays like a plain spring-damper.

atoms.idea: Benefits: Kp, Kv are directly in task coordinates, and only J and its inverse are needed, not f⁻¹.
atoms.feynman: Tune stiffness in the directions the job cares about, like a stiff pen sideways and soft pen up-down.
atoms.visual: Kp shown as a gold ellipse at the hand: stretch it in x vs y and the hand's response becomes stiffer in that direction.

atoms.idea: Near a singularity of the coordinates x, M̃ grows large: some directions barely move under large forces. This singularity is an artifact of the parametrization, not of joint space.
atoms.feynman: An outstretched arm can barely push further outward: it feels infinitely heavy in that direction.
atoms.visual: Stretch the arm straight: the M̃ ellipse blows up along the arm's direction (🚫 flash), while joint-space dials show nothing special.

atoms.label: Ex 4.8
atoms.idea: Example: planar 2-DOF arm with hand xy as workspace variables, comparing joint-space and workspace computed torque.
atoms.feynman: Two ways to steer the same pen to the same dot.
atoms.visual: Race mode setup: two copies of the arm, same start and same gold goal.

atoms.feynman: Moving each joint smoothly bends the fingertip's path.
atoms.visual: Left copy: orange joint traces in time are clean damped curves; the pink hand trail curves.

pages.summary: Figures 4.10 and 4.11: step responses of joint-space and workspace computed torque controllers in joint and Cartesian coordinates.

atoms.idea: Joint-space computed torque step: straight-line path with overshoot in joint coordinates, curved path in Cartesian coordinates; θ1, θ2 versus time are underdamped responses.
atoms.feynman: Moving shoulder and elbow evenly sweeps the hand along an arc.

atoms.idea: Section 4.6 Control of Constrained Manipulators.
A brief treatment; the full version is in Chapter 6.
atoms.feynman: A first taste of touching the world.
atoms.visual: Preview: the arm's hand slides along a slate wall with a purple push arrow.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.6.1 Dynamics of constrained systems.

atoms.label: Eq (4.56)-(4.57)
atoms.idea: Task: slide the tip along a frictionless surface while pressing on it. The surface in joint space is k independent constraints hⱼ(θ) = 0, parametrized by an injective map θ = f(φ), φ ∈ R^{n−k}.
atoms.feynman: A train on a track: the track is a rule on where it can be; distance along the track is the only free knob.
atoms.visual: Joint-space plane (θ1, θ2) with the constraint drawn as a slate curve h = 0; a φ slider moves a teal dot along it, and the real arm's hand moves along the slot correspondingly.

atoms.label: Eq (4.58)
atoms.idea: Normals to the surface are spanned by the gradients ∇hⱼ (k of them); torques τN = Σ λⱼ∇hⱼ(θ) push against the surface.
atoms.feynman: Pushing a drawer straight into its side rail doesn't slide it; it only presses.
atoms.visual: At the teal dot on the curve, purple normal arrows ∇h; a λ slider scales a purple τN arrow along them.

atoms.idea: Without friction, normal torques do no work: τN·θ̇ = Σλᵢ ∇hᵢ·θ̇ = Σλᵢ d/dt h(θ) = 0, so they cause no motion; the desired λ(t) is part of the task.
atoms.feynman: Pressing a sliding puck down onto ice changes nothing about how it slides.
atoms.visual: Power meter τN·θ̇ stays at zero while the dot slides along the curve and the purple arrow pushes perpendicular; a gold λ target line sits on the λ slider.

atoms.idea: If contact is kept, the dynamics can be written in φ.
atoms.feynman: Describe the train's motion by distance along the track.
atoms.visual: The φ slider becomes the main dial; the 2D joint plane fades back.

atoms.idea: Page 200.

pages.summary: Substituting θ = f(φ) into the dynamics, projecting by Jᵀ gives M̃φ̈ + C̃φ̇ + Ñ = F with the same structure; projection discards constraint forces; control task stated.

atoms.label: Eq (4.59)
atoms.idea: θ̇ = (∂f/∂φ)φ̇ and θ̈ = (∂f/∂φ)φ̈ + d/dt(∂f/∂φ)φ̇.
atoms.feynman: Joint speeds follow from speed along the track, through the track's shape.
atoms.visual: Drag φ̇: orange joint-speed arrows appear tangent to the slate curve.

atoms.label: Eq (4.60)
atoms.idea: Substituting: M(∂f/∂φ)φ̈ + (C ∂f/∂φ + M d/dt ∂f/∂φ)φ̇ + N = τ.
atoms.feynman: The arm's rulebook rewritten for track distance.
atoms.visual: The four torque bars recomputed with φ as the knob; a purple leftover bar shows what the slot must supply.

atoms.label: Eq (4.61)-(4.62)
atoms.idea: Premultiply by Jᵀ with J = ∂f/∂φ: M̃ = JᵀMJ, C̃ = Jᵀ(CJ + MJ̇), Ñ = JᵀN, F = Jᵀτ, giving M̃φ̈ + C̃φ̇ + Ñ = F.
atoms.feynman: Only the part of your push along the track matters for how the train moves.
atoms.visual: A projector: torque vectors cast a shadow onto the lime tangent direction; the shadow length is F and drives the φ motion.

atoms.idea: This has the same form as unconstrained dynamics and satisfies Lemma 4.2 (Chapter 6), unsurprising since φ are generalized coordinates for the constrained system.
atoms.feynman: The train on its track is just a simpler machine with one knob.
atoms.visual: Skew badge and positive-inertia badge appear on the projected equation with lime checks.

atoms.idea: Projection holds only on h = 0 and discards constraint forces; to regulate them, use the full equation (4.60).
atoms.feynman: The shadow tells you how the train moves but not how hard it presses on the rails.
atoms.visual: The purple normal component of τ is greyed out by the projector, with a coral flag: needed for force control.

atoms.idea: Subsection 4.6.2 Control of constrained manipulators.
Goal: regulate position along the surface and force against it simultaneously; stability needs only the motion along the surface since none occurs normal to it.
atoms.feynman: Wipe the table: control where the cloth goes and how hard you press, two separate jobs.
atoms.visual: Two gold targets: a position marker on the slot and a force level on the λ gauge; two error meters appear.

atoms.idea: Page 201.

atoms.idea: This assumes contact is kept; without a physical constraint the force must always push into, never pull away from, the surface.
atoms.feynman: Wiping a table only works while the cloth touches it; press down, never lift.
atoms.visual: Wall mode: if λ goes negative (pulling), the hand separates from the slate wall and a coral flash appears.

atoms.idea: The computed-torque approach is extended to position and force; only a sketch is given, with hybrid control as a special case of the general interaction problem in Chapter 6.

atoms.idea: Section 4.7 Summary.
Recap 1: any system with Lagrangian L = T − V in generalized coordinates obeys d/dt ∂L/∂q̇ − ∂L/∂q = Υ.
atoms.feynman: Energy bookkeeping predicts motion: momentum changes as hills and outside pushes say.
atoms.visual: Roadmap station 'energy → motion' lights, showing the spherical pendulum thumbnail with its Lagrange bars.

atoms.idea: Recap 2: a rigid body obeys the body-frame Newton–Euler equation with block inertia diag(mI, I), body twist and body wrench.
atoms.feynman: Push and spin of a floating brick, in the brick's own frame.
atoms.visual: Station 'push and spin' lights with the tumbling brick thumbnail.

atoms.idea: Recap 3: open-chain arms obey M(θ)θ̈ + C(θ, θ̇)θ̇ + N = τ, with M symmetric positive definite and Ṁ − 2C skew-symmetric.
atoms.feynman: Heaviness, fling, weight and muscles always balance; the fling never makes free energy.
atoms.visual: Station 'arm mass matrix' lights with the four balancing torque bars and the zero power meter.

atoms.idea: Recap 4: asymptotic stability via Lyapunov's direct method (V lpdf, −V̇ lpdf), LaSalle when −V̇ is only semidefinite, or the indirect method via linearization.
atoms.feynman: Ball in a bowl that keeps losing energy; or zoom in and check that every wiggle dies.
atoms.visual: Three stability stations light: bowl, magnet, magnifier.
